docs.text: Family Inductive Bias Interaction Mechanism Complexity (length \(L\)) Edge Hardware Affinity CNN Locality & translation equivariance Sliding window, receptive field grows linearly Time \(O(L)\), Memory \(O(L)\) Very high (weight reuse, structured memory access, NPU friendly) Transformer Minimal bias (permutation equivariant, needs PE) All-to-all content addressing (dynamic soft routing) Time \(O(L^2)\), Memory \(O(L^2)\) Demands acceleration (KV Cache bandwidth bound during generation) SSM / Mamba Continuous recurrence & state dynamics Selective continuous compression & hidden update Training \(O(L)\), Step inference \(O(1)\) Good (no expanding KV cache footprint during generation) GNN Topological invariance & permutation equivariance Message passing along explicit graph edges Depends on sparsity & sampling Moderate (irregular memory access and sparse matrix operations)

docs.title: Vision, Multimodality & 3D Space
docs.text:
What this page solves

Vision tasks extend from "what is it" (classification) to "where" (detection, segmentation), "how far and how big" (depth, 3D) and "how to describe it in language" (vision-language). This is the core of robot perception and many industrial AI roles. P1: tasks and metrics required; P2: go deep into 3D by direction.

docs.title: Knowledge map
docs.text: Level Topic What to understand P1 Classification, detection, segmentation Labels, boxes, pixel masks and their metrics; CNN / ViT, YOLO / DETR, promptable segmentation P1 Vision-language and video Image-text alignment, VLMs, temporal context P2 3D geometry and representations Depth, point clouds, pose, occupancy / SDF, NeRF, 3D Gaussian splatting P2 Space and interaction Geometric reconstruction, semantics, affordances and action conditioning

docs.title: Core mechanics
docs.text:
From classification to detection to segmentation: classification outputs one label; detection outputs boxes plus classes (YOLO: one-stage, fast; Faster R-CNN: two-stage, accurate; DETR: a Transformer predicting the box set directly, no NMS); semantic segmentation classifies every pixel, and instance segmentation also separates individuals of the same class (Mask R-CNN, YOLO-seg).

Metrics: IoU is intersection-over-union of prediction and ground truth; mAP integrates the precision-recall curve ranked by confidence, then averages over classes and IoU thresholds. Segmentation often uses mIoU.

ViT: cut the image into 16×16 patches as tokens for a Transformer. Weaker than CNNs on little data (no locality prior), stronger with lots; CNNs are still friendlier on edge devices.

Promptable segmentation (SAM): given a point or box, segment the object, with no class-specific training. Suits labelling and new objects in robotics.

Depth and 3D: monocular depth (e.g. Depth Anything), stereo, RGB-D; 3D representations include point clouds, meshes, voxels, SDFs; NeRF represents a scene implicitly with a network and renders new views; 3D Gaussian splatting uses many coloured Gaussian ellipsoids explicitly and renders far faster.

Vision-language: CLIP aligns image and text spaces; VLMs feed visual tokens into a language model (see the multimodal topic in Foundation Models).

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
What separates mAP@0.5 from mAP@0.5:0.95 for detection?

The first counts a prediction correct at IoU ≥ 0.5; the second averages over ten thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 and is much stricter about localisation.

Why does ViT often lose to CNNs on small datasets?

CNNs have built-in locality and translation-invariance priors, so little data suffices; ViT's priors are weak and need large data or strong pretraining to learn these regularities.

Main difference between NeRF and 3D Gaussian splatting?

NeRF is an implicit MLP; rendering queries the network many times per ray, which is slow. 3DGS uses explicit Gaussian ellipsoids with rasterisation, rendering in real time but using more storage.

docs.title: Search, Planning & Decision Learning
docs.text:
What this page solves

AI does not only predict; it chooses actions under states, constraints and feedback. This page separates search and planning, imitation and reinforcement learning — the common base of robot policies, world models and agents. P1: know it; RL is an optional deep dive.

docs.title: Knowledge map
docs.text: Level Topic What to understand P1 Classical decision and symbolic methods Search, heuristics, constraints, knowledge representation P1 Reinforcement learning MDP, value, policy, reward, exploration; DQN, policy gradient, PPO P1 Imitation and offline learning Behaviour cloning, distribution shift; offline RL vs supervised learning P2 Models, reasoning and interaction Model-based RL, world models, hierarchical skills, multi-agent

docs.title: Core mechanics
docs.text:
Markov decision process (MDP): state s, action a, transition P(s'|s,a), reward r, discount γ. The goal is a policy π(a|s) maximising expected cumulative discounted reward.

Value functions: V(s) is the expected return from state s; Q(s,a) is the expected return after taking action a and then following the policy. The Bellman equation writes them as "current reward + discounted value of the next state" — the core of almost every RL algorithm.

Value-based methods: Q-learning updates Q iteratively with the Bellman equation; DQN approximates Q with a network plus experience replay (breaks sample correlation) and a target network (stabilises the target). Suits discrete actions.

Policy gradient and actor-critic: optimise policy parameters directly, handling continuous actions; a critic's value estimate serves as a baseline to cut variance. PPO limits each policy update, is stable and practical, and is the default for robot RL and RLHF.

Exploration vs exploitation: always taking the best-known action misses better ones; ε-greedy, entropy regularisation and curiosity rewards are common exploration tools. With sparse rewards, exploration is the hardest part.

Imitation vs reinforcement: imitation learns from demonstrations, needs no reward but is limited by demo coverage; RL learns from reward, can exceed the demos, but is sample-inefficient and rewards are hard to design. Offline RL uses only a fixed dataset with no interaction; the difficulty is over-optimistic values for out-of-data actions.

Model-based RL: learn an environment model (world model) first and plan or generate data in it; sample-efficient, but the policy can exploit model errors.

docs.title: Follow-along · AI-4 · CartPole with repeated evaluation
docs.text:
1. Run the official example; mark environment, observation, action, reward and termination.
  2. Separate the exploration policy used in training from the evaluation policy; save checkpoints.
  3. At least three training seeds; fix evaluation conditions and report the return distribution over many episodes.
  4. Change only one hyperparameter or perturbation; record training and inference cost and failures.

Done when: starts on a CPU; one success video is not evidence of stability. For robotics, do imitation learning E3 first; RL is a separate branch.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why does DQN need experience replay and a target network?

Consecutive samples are highly correlated, making direct training unstable; replay shuffles them. The target network fixes the TD target for a while so the network is not chasing its own tail.

Why report RL results over several random seeds?

RL is very sensitive to initialisation and exploration; one algorithm's spread across seeds can exceed the gap between algorithms, so a single seed is not trustworthy.

Why can't offline RL just use ordinary Q-learning?

For actions absent from the dataset, Q estimates may be overestimated; the policy picks those actions and never gets to correct them through interaction.

docs.title: Definition of Decision Trees
docs.text:
A decision tree is a supervised learning algorithm used for classification and regression. It builds a tree-like model by splitting the dataset into smaller subsets, enabling predictions to be made based on the data. Each internal node represents a test on a feature, and each leaf node represents a class label or a numerical value.

The process of building a decision tree typically involves the following steps:

  1. Feature Selection: Use a criterion (e.g., information gain, Gini index) to select the feature that best separates the data.
  2. Data Splitting: Split the dataset into subsets based on the selected feature.
  3. Recursive Subtree Construction: Repeat the above steps for each subset until a stopping condition is met (e.g., maximum depth or minimum number of samples per leaf).
  4. Tree Generation: Combine all subtrees into a complete decision tree.
  5. Pruning: Simplify the tree by removing some unnecessary branches to prevent overfitting.
  6. Prediction: Use the resulting decision tree to make predictions on new data.

docs.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Decision Trees
Advantages
docs.text:
• Easy to Understand and Interpret: The structure of a decision tree is intuitive and easy to visualize and explain.
  • Handles Nonlinear Relationships: Capable of modeling nonlinear interactions between features.
  • No Need for Feature Scaling: Standardization or normalization of features is not required.
  • Suitable for Large Datasets: Can handle large-scale datasets and has relatively fast training speed.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Overfitting: Decision trees are prone to overfitting, especially when the tree is deep.
  • Instability: Small changes in the data can lead to significant changes in the tree structure.
  • Bias Toward Multivalued Features: Trees may favor features with more categories.
  • Limited in Capturing Complex Patterns: May struggle to model more intricate patterns in data.

docs.title: Core mechanistic intuition · Reliability & evaluation
docs.text:
• Confidence vs. correctness: Modern deep neural networks with Softmax output are routinely overconfident. Calibration (e.g., Temperature Scaling) measures whether predicted probabilities align with observed empirical frequencies.
  • Out-of-Distribution (OOD) & domain shift: Identical distribution (i.i.d.) is the fundamental premise of empirical risk minimization. When sensor drift or environmental conditions change, performance can degrade abruptly; density or reconstruction-based rejection filters are essential.
  • Hidden leakage pathways: Leakage extends far beyond identical sample duplication. Preprocessing statistics computed across the entire corpus, random splits on autocorrelated time series, and cross-split sensor contamination yield illusory benchmark results.

docs.title: Core mechanistic intuition · From classical ML to neural nets
docs.text:
• Feature space & inductive bias: Linear models assume hyperplane separation; decision trees perform axis-aligned orthogonal partitions (invariant to monotonic feature scaling); kernel SVMs map to implicit reproducing Hilbert spaces; neural networks learn continuous coordinate warpings via layered function compositions.
  • Optimization & backprop: Backpropagation is dynamic programming caching intermediate jacobians of the chain rule. Gradient descent stability depends on the curvature (Hessian conditioning) of the loss surface—the primary reason learning rate warmup, normalization layers, and adaptive moment estimation (Adam) are required.

docs.title: Geometric Representation & Generative Modelling
docs.text:
What this page solves

How models generate new data, and what geometric structure data itself has. Manifolds and latent spaces describe data and representations; diffusion and flow matching are generation methods — and the mathematical basis of robot diffusion policies and π0-style VLA action heads. Topic elective: not a shared prerequisite for LLM or robotics entry.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
• Manifolds & latent spaces

    What low-dimensional structure hides in high-dimensional data? Ambient space, intrinsic dimension, latent variables.

    Open topic

  • Diffusion models

    Learn denoising and the score across noise levels, then sample step by step.

    Open topic

  • Flow matching

    Learn a velocity field from noise to data and generate by ODE integration.

    Open topic

docs.title: Core mechanics · the landscape of generative methods
docs.text:
Every generative model answers one question: how to turn samples from a simple distribution (usually Gaussian noise) into samples from the data distribution. They differ in how they transport:

Family Core idea Strength Cost Autoregressive Factor the joint into conditionals, generate in order Simple training, exact likelihood Slow, sequential VAE Encode to latents and decode, optimise the ELBO Explicit latent space Blurrier samples GAN A generator fools a discriminator Sharp, fast samples Unstable training, mode collapse Normalizing flow Invertible maps with exact density change Exact likelihood Architectures constrained by invertibility Diffusion / score Learn step-by-step denoising (the log-density gradient) High quality, stable, multi-modal Many sampling steps Flow matching Regress the velocity field from noise to data Simpler training, straighter paths, fewer steps possible Still needs numerical integration

A Transformer is an architecture; diffusion and flow matching are generation methods — a Transformer can be their denoising network (e.g. DiT). The manifold hypothesis is a way of viewing data, not a generation algorithm.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
What are the main problems of diffusion models and GANs?

GANs train unstably and mode-collapse (generating only a few kinds of samples); diffusion trains stably and covers the distribution but needs tens to thousands of sampling steps.

Why do robot action generators use diffusion or flow matching instead of regression?

One state may allow several valid actions (a multi-modal distribution); regression outputs their average, while diffusion / flow matching samples one valid mode.

Why does latent diffusion (e.g. Stable Diffusion) encode to a latent space first?

Pixel space is high-dimensional and expensive; a VAE compresses to a small latent space, diffusion runs there, and the decoder maps back — far less compute.

docs.title: Diffusion Models
docs.text:
What this page solves

Generate data by denoising pure noise step by step. Diffusion is the mainstream for image and video generation and the basis of robot diffusion policies. Topic elective; read the ideas of noising, denoising and sampling first; coding needs basic probability, gradients and PyTorch.

docs.title: Core mechanics
docs.text:
Forward noising: add Gaussian noise step by step until, after T steps, the data is nearly pure noise. The noised sample at any t has a closed form: x_t = √ᾱ_t · x_0 + √(1−ᾱ_t) · ε, so training never actually iterates.

Training objective: the network takes x_t and t and predicts the added noise ε (equivalently the score, the gradient of the log density), with mean-squared error. One network serves all noise levels, so t is a required input.

Reverse sampling: start from noise and remove part of the predicted noise each step, walking back to the data distribution. DDPM is stochastic per step; DDIM is deterministic and allows fewer steps.

The score view: the score ∇log p(x) points towards denser data. Diffusion learns the score at many noise scales and follows it (Langevin dynamics).

Conditional generation: add class, text, image or robot observations as inputs. Classifier-free guidance trains conditional and unconditional models together and amplifies their difference at sampling, strengthening the condition at the cost of diversity.

Faster sampling: deterministic solvers (DDIM, DPM-Solver), consistency models and distillation compress thousands of steps to a few or one.

Diffusion is not a particular U-Net or Transformer; and "stochastic vs deterministic" does not separate diffusion from flow matching — both can sample deterministically.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why can training compute the noised sample at any t directly?

Repeatedly adding Gaussian noise stays Gaussian with closed-form mean and variance, so x_t follows from x_0 and one noise sample.

What happens with a larger classifier-free guidance scale?

Samples follow the condition (e.g. the text) more closely but lose diversity and may over-saturate or distort.

How do noise prediction and score prediction relate?

They differ only by a noise-level-dependent scale and sign: score ≈ −ε / √(1−ᾱ_t).

docs.title: Flow Matching
docs.text:
Prerequisites and role

Use vectors, probability basics, time-dependent functions, numerical ODEs and PyTorch. Begin with 2D distribution transport before large image or robot applications.

docs.title: Intuition: learn how points move over time
docs.text:
Choose a probability path from a simple distribution toward data, then learn a time-dependent vector field. Generate by drawing initial points and integrating the learned field with an ODE solver.

A common teaching setup draws a noise endpoint \(x_0\) and data endpoint \(x_1\), constructs \(x_t=(1-t)x_0+t x_1\), and regresses conditional velocity \(x_1-x_0\). Here \(t=0\) is noise and \(t=1\) is data; specify paths, endpoint coupling and time convention.

This is one conditional path choice. Sampling does not know a destination data point, and learned trajectories need not all be straight. Training can regress a constructible target; generation still requires numerical integration.

docs.title: Related concepts
docs.text:
Concept Relationship Diffusion / score matching Commonly use noise levels and denoising/score objectives; connections to flows exist under appropriate assumptions Flow matching Commonly fit a velocity field for a probability path; path choices affect learning and sampling Normalizing flow A family of invertible distribution transformations, not a synonym for the flow-matching objective Rectified flow Related to specific paths and velocity learning, not a generic name for every flow-matching method

Speed and quality depend on models, data, solvers and steps. The name alone does not establish faster sampling or replacement of diffusion.

docs.title: Core mechanistic intuition · Simulation-free training vs. numerical ODE sampling
docs.text:
• Training phase (Simulation-free regression):
    • Sample noise point \(x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) and clean data point \(x_1 \sim q(x)\).
    • Interpolate along a straight conditional path: \(x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1\).
    • Target conditional velocity field is constant: \(u_t(x|x_1, x_0) = \frac{d x_t}{d t} = x_1 - x_0\).
    • The neural network simply minimizes MSE: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, x_1} \left[ \| v_\theta(x_t, t) - (x_1 - x_0) \|^2 \right]\). No expensive numerical ODE simulation is required during training.
  • Sampling phase (ODE integration):
    • Sample initial point \(x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\).
    • Numerically integrate the ODE \(\frac{d x_t}{d t} = v_\theta(x_t, t)\) using Euler, Midpoint, or RK4 solvers from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\) to synthesize clean sample \(x_1\).
  • Contrast with diffusion: Diffusion models typically evolve along curved, noisy stochastic trajectories. Flow matching with optimal-transport paths yields straighter probability trajectories, enabling high-fidelity generation in substantially fewer numerical solver steps (e.g., 10–20 steps).

docs.title: Same course, experiment G3
docs.text:
Use MIT 6.S184, 2026, lectures 1–2 and the flow-matching section of Lab 2, sharing code and notation with G2.

  1. Identify noise, data, sampled time and conditional paths.
  2. Plot paths, derive the target and train the original 2D example.
  3. Visualize vector fields at multiple times and trajectories from fixed initial noise.
  4. Vary solver steps; record distributions, trajectories and sampling time.
  5. When comparing G2/G3, match data, capacity and evaluation where possible and report training/sampling costs separately.

Acceptance: explain information available during training vs. sampling, plus one step/path experiment and failure analysis. State limitations when comparison settings differ.

docs.title: Check yourself · Critical thinking
docs.text:
• Why can training regress on conditional straight-line velocity targets without simulation, while sampling must integrate through the marginalized nonlinear field?
  • Why are the empirical inference trajectories of \(v_\theta(x, t)\) not guaranteed to be strictly linear, even when trained on straight conditional paths?
  • In embodied policy learning (Action Flow / Diffusion Policy), why is flow matching better suited to capturing multimodal demonstrations than direct MSE regression?

docs.title: Manifolds & Latent Spaces
docs.text:
What this page solves

Why high-dimensional data is often "not really that high-dimensional", and what a learned latent space means. Your geometry and linear-algebra background carries over, and the latent state in your Manifold Dynamics work belongs to this view. Topic elective; no differential geometry or topology needed in round one.

docs.title: Core mechanics
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Caution Ambient space Where the raw numbers live A 224×224 colour image is a 150,000-dimensional vector Manifold A space locally described by low-dimensional Euclidean coordinates Complex data need not form one smooth manifold Manifold hypothesis Real data concentrates near low-dimensional structure A useful modelling assumption to check against data Latent space Internal variables a model uses or learns Not guaranteed low-dimensional, interpretable or geometry-preserving

The Swiss-roll lesson: points live in 3D, yet variation along the rolled surface needs only two parameters. Straight-line 3D distance wrongly makes neighbours of points on adjacent layers; distance along the surface (geodesic) reflects true similarity.

Linear vs non-linear reduction: PCA finds directions of maximum variance and cannot unroll a curled manifold; Isomap, LLE and UMAP unroll using local neighbourhoods. In t-SNE and UMAP plots, distances between clusters and cluster sizes usually mean nothing.

Networks and representations: a deep network can be seen as a chain of coordinate transforms that pulls tangled classes apart layer by layer until they are linearly separable. Good representations make downstream tasks easy.

docs.text:

docs.title: G1: unrolling curled data
docs.text:
1. Run the official Swiss-roll example and check the colour-to-point correspondence.
  2. State the ambient dimension and the generating parameter dimension.
  3. Add PCA as a linear baseline and compare with the chosen non-linear method.
  4. Change only the neighbour count or noise; see whether unrolling breaks neighbourhoods, short-circuits or splits.
  5. Save the point cloud, 2D embedding and parameters; compare local structure on held-out neighbourhood checks, not just how nice the plot looks.

Done when: at least three settings, local neighbourhoods vs global shape explained; a 2D plot does not prove a "true manifold" was found.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why can't PCA unroll the Swiss roll?

PCA is a linear projection onto the plane of maximum variance; a curled structure needs a non-linear map, and projecting presses layers together.

What happens when k neighbours is too large?

Neighbourhoods span adjacent layers and short-circuit, linking far-apart points, so the unrolled result folds or scrambles.

Why not judge how different two clusters are from their distance in a t-SNE plot?

t-SNE preserves only local neighbourhoods; inter-cluster distance and cluster size depend heavily on parameters and do not reflect the original space.

docs.title: Must-know interview questions (answer key)
docs.text: Question Key points Why residual connections? Gradients bypass the non-linear layers, so deep networks optimise more easily; each layer learns an increment BatchNorm vs LayerNorm? BN normalises across the batch, depends on batch size and uses running statistics at inference; LN normalises across features, suits sequences and small batches; Transformers use LN Complexity of self-attention, and how to reduce it? O(n²) time and memory in sequence length; sparse / linear attention, FlashAttention (same complexity, far less memory traffic), state-space models (Mamba, linear) Adam or SGD? Adam converges fast and tolerates learning-rate choice; SGD + momentum often generalises better in vision; large models use AdamW (decoupled weight decay) What is data leakage? Test information reaching training or model selection, e.g. random splits of time series or normalising on all data; metrics become inflated How is mAP computed? Sort by confidence, build the PR curve, integrate to AP, average over classes (and IoU thresholds) PTQ vs QAT? PTQ sets scales from a small calibration set after training: fast, may lose accuracy. QAT simulates quantisation error during training: better accuracy, needs retraining INT8 lost accuracy — how to debug? Compare per-layer outputs before and after quantisation to find sensitive layers (often first/last and outlier-heavy ones); per-channel scales, different calibration, or keep a few layers in FP16 Why are fewer FLOPs not always faster? Many layers are memory-bound, not compute-bound; operator fusion and support in the runtime decide real latency First things to check for edge deployment? Memory (weights + peak activations), latency target, operator support, power; then choose model size and quantisation

docs.title: Graph Learning & Geometric Deep Learning
docs.text:
What this page solves

Put relations, topology and symmetry explicitly into the model. It meets your sensor networks (spatial relations between nodes), point clouds and 3D geometry, but graph structure must be justified by the task or data — not used for its own sake. P1: know it; P2: go deep by direction.

docs.title: Knowledge map
docs.text: Level Topic What to understand P1 Graph basics and tasks Nodes, edges, adjacency; node-, edge- and graph-level prediction; permutation invariance and equivariance P1 Message passing GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT; neighbourhood aggregation, sampling and features P2 Modern geometric methods Graph Transformers, positional encodings, point clouds and SE(3)-equivariant models P2 Limits and scientific use Over-smoothing, over-squashing, graph-construction leakage; molecules, sensor graphs, physical fields

docs.title: Core mechanics
docs.text:
Message passing: in each layer every node collects its neighbours' features (messages), aggregates them (sum, mean or attention-weighted) and combines with its own to update. After k layers a node "sees" information within k hops.

Permutation invariance and equivariance: graphs have no natural node order, so aggregation must be order-independent. Graph-level outputs should be invariant; node-level outputs should reorder along with the nodes (equivariant).

GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT: GCN averages with degree normalisation; GraphSAGE samples neighbours and works on nodes unseen in training (inductive); GAT learns per-neighbour weights with attention.

Over-smoothing and over-squashing: with many layers all node representations converge (over-smoothing); distant information must squeeze through few paths and is lost (over-squashing). So GNNs are usually shallow.

Geometric equivariant networks: properties of point clouds and molecules should not change under global rotation and translation. SE(3)-equivariant networks build the symmetry into the structure, needing less data than learning it through augmentation.

Transductive vs inductive: transductive trains and tests on the same graph (only labels are hidden); inductive must generalise to new graphs or nodes. State which one you evaluate, and never use test labels when building the graph.

docs.title: Follow-along · AI-3 · What does graph structure actually add?
docs.text:
1. Run the PyG example; understand x, edge_index, labels and data masks.
  2. On the same split, compare an MLP that ignores edges with a GCN.
  3. Perturb some edges and record validation and test results; avoid leaking test labels when rebuilding the graph.
  4. State whether the example is transductive or inductive, then discuss sensor applications.

Done when: starts on a CPU with a small graph; report the baseline, edge perturbation, masks and limits, without equating node classification with structural damage identification.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why are GNNs usually only a few layers deep?

More layers over-smooth node representations until they are indistinguishable and over-squash distant information. For long-range information use graph Transformers, virtual nodes or skip connections.

How do you show the graph structure really helps?

Compare against an edge-free MLP on the same split, then shuffle or delete some edges and check that performance drops accordingly.

What to watch when modelling a sensor network as a graph?

Edge definitions (physical connection, distance threshold or correlation) need justification; building edges from correlations computed on all data leaks test information into the model.

docs.title: Mamba & State-Space Sequence Models
docs.text:
What this page solves

Understand another family of sequence models through "how the state updates, how history is compressed, how compute scales with length". Your familiarity with state-space equations and system identification is a strong start, and you have already swapped Transformer for Mamba in a tunnelling project. P1: know it; P2: go deep.

docs.title: Core mechanics
docs.text:
Linear state-space model: continuous form h'(t) = A h(t) + B x(t), y(t) = C h(t). After discretisation (e.g. zero-order hold) it becomes the recurrence h_t = Ā h_{t−1} + B̄ x_t — the same state equation as in control theory.

Two ways to compute: when A, B, C do not depend on the input (LTI, e.g. S4), the recurrence unrolls into one long convolution for parallel training; inference uses the recurrence, O(1) per step with no cache growing with length.

Selectivity (Mamba's key idea): make B, C and the step size Δ depend on the current input, so the model decides what to remember and what to ignore — fixing LTI models' inability to select by content. The cost: no convolution form, so a hardware-aware parallel scan is used instead.

Trade-off against attention: attention keeps all history and can look back exactly at any position, but its KV cache grows with length; an SSM compresses history into a fixed-size state, saving memory and speeding long-sequence inference, but is weaker at exact recall of distant detail. Hence hybrids (a few attention layers + many SSM layers) are increasingly common.

Mamba-2 and SSD: shows a duality between structured SSMs and a class of linear attention, with better training efficiency.

Not a physical state: the SSM "state" is a learned abstract vector, not necessarily a real physical state; do not read it as an interpretable system-identification result.

Level Topic Distinguish P1 Linear state space, discretisation, recurrence Mathematical state ≠ physical state P1 Selective SSM / Mamba Input-dependent selection, not a fixed linear filter P2 Mamba-2, SSD, hybrid sequence models Structural links, training and inference cost, accuracy P2 Time-series and long-sequence use Data, sampling rate, length and task set the comparison

docs.title: Small experiment: build a comparable baseline first
docs.text:
On data from the time-series & scientific AI topic (see related topics below), first compare persistence / linear prediction with a small network; then add Mamba, fixing time split, input window, training budget and device, and record prediction quality, latency and memory.

Done when: you can explain state compression vs attention's access to history, without claiming Mamba is faster in practice or has replaced Transformers from asymptotic complexity alone.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why can an LTI SSM be written as a convolution but Mamba cannot?

In an LTI model Ā, B̄, C are fixed, so the output is the input convolved with one fixed kernel; Mamba's parameters change with the input, so each step's "kernel" differs and only a scan works.

In long-sequence inference, where does Mamba save over a Transformer?

A Transformer's KV cache grows linearly with length and each new token reads the whole cache; Mamba keeps a fixed-size state, so per-step compute and memory are constant.

On what tasks might Mamba lose to attention?

Tasks that require exact copying or retrieval of specific distant content (e.g. finding a phone number in a long document): a fixed-size state struggles to keep every detail losslessly.

Continue Lee/Karpathy as existing backbones. Use CS231n for vision and representations and MIT 6.S184 for generation. Enter graph/RL courses only after selecting those directions; use official walkthroughs for small experiments.

Each topic normally has one primary entry and one necessary practical/reference entry. docs.title: Representation Learning & Learning Paradigms
docs.text:
What this page solves

How features are learned and where the supervision signal comes from. Most of modern AI's capability comes from "learn a good representation on lots of unlabelled data first, then transfer to a specific task". P0: transfer learning is required; P1: know self-supervision.

docs.title: Knowledge map
docs.text: Level Topic What to understand P0 Representations, embeddings, transfer Features, similarity, frozen encoder, linear probe, fine-tuning, domain shift P1 Self-supervised & contrastive learning Augmented views, positives/negatives, representation collapse P1 Masked, teacher and predictive representations How MAE, DINO and JEPA objectives differ P2 Continual, active, few-shot, federated learning Forgetting, labelling budget, distributed privacy; pick by task

docs.title: Core mechanics
docs.text:
Representation and transfer: a good representation puts similar inputs close in vector space, so a downstream task needs only a simple head on top. A linear probe (freeze the encoder, train one linear layer) measures representation quality; full fine-tuning usually does better but needs more data and compute and overfits more easily.

Contrastive learning: two augmented views of the same image are positives to pull together; different images are negatives to push apart (SimCLR). CLIP applies the same idea to image-text pairs. The key risk is representation collapse — every input maps to one point and the loss can still be low.

Masked prediction: hide part of the input and make the model fill it in. BERT masks words, MAE masks image patches (still learns well with 75% masked). No negatives needed.

Teacher-student and self-distillation: DINO makes a student match a momentum-updated teacher's outputs across views; no negatives, no collapse, and the features segment semantically well.

Predictive representations (JEPA): predict the masked part in representation space rather than pixel space, so capacity is not wasted reconstructing irrelevant detail — close to the world-model idea.

Domain shift: when training and deployment distributions differ (lighting, devices, scenes), transfer breaks. Moving structural monitoring from lab to field is a textbook domain shift.

docs.text:

docs.title: Follow-along · AI-2 · frozen features vs full fine-tuning
docs.text:
1. Run the original transfer-learning example; confirm pretrained weights and augmentation.
  2. On the same data split, compare a frozen encoder with full fine-tuning.
  3. Reduce training labels or change image conditions; observe accuracy and training cost.
  4. Explain why better accuracy alone does not prove causal or complete semantics were learned.

Done when: training curves, validation results, time and failure cases; doable after F1, easier with a small GPU.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
With very little labelled data, freeze the encoder or fine-tune fully?

Usually freeze first (or fine-tune only the last layers): fewer parameters, less overfitting; unfreeze gradually as data grows.

What is representation collapse in contrastive learning, and how is it avoided?

Every input maps to the same vector; the alignment loss is zero but there is no information. Avoid it with negatives (SimCLR), asymmetric structure with a momentum teacher (BYOL, DINO) or variance regularisation (VICReg).

Why can MAE mask 75% of image patches?

Images are highly redundant; at low mask ratios neighbouring pixels let the model interpolate. A high ratio forces higher-level structure, and the encoder sees only visible patches, so training is faster.

docs.text: This directly connects signals, identification and structural research. Start temporal splits and classical baselines, then distinguish data prediction, physical constraints and operator learning.

docs.title: Map and priority
docs.text: Depth Topic Understand P1 Time-series tasks and baselines Forecasting, classification, anomalies and imputation; persistence/linear models, frequency features and leakage P1 Temporal networks TCN, RNN, Transformers and SSM; locality, long range and multivariate inputs P2 Time-series foundation models Pretraining data, sample rates, normalization, transfer and uncertainty P2 PINNs and inverse problems Equation/boundary residuals as losses; accuracy and superiority require validation P2 Neural operators and hybrids FNO/DeepONet learn function maps; test resolution, parameters and conservation

docs.title: Core mechanistic intuition · From temporal representations to physical operators
docs.text:
• Evolution of deep time series:
    1. Recurrent models (RNN/LSTM): Hidden state recurrence, prone to vanishing gradients, struggles with long-range vibrational phase preservation.
    2. Point-wise self-attention (Vanilla Time Transformer): Treating each timestamp as a token disrupts temporal continuity, risks overfitting noise, and incurs quadratic cost on long sensor records.
    3. Patching & Channel Independence (PatchTST/iTransformer): Aggregating consecutive time steps into sub-series patches preserves local context. Treating channels independently or projecting variables as tokens significantly improves generalization across sensor arrays.
  • PINNs vs. Neural Operators (FNO/DeepONet):
    • PINN (Loss-constrained): Parameterizes a specific trajectory \(u(t, x)\) under given parameters, penalized by PDE/ODE residuals. Requires no vast dataset but needs re-optimization per condition, often vulnerable to loss landscape imbalances.
    • Neural Operators (Operator mapping): Maps between infinite-dimensional function spaces (e.g., input excitation force field \(\to\) structural response field). Fourier layers compute global convolutions in spectral space, achieving mesh independence (zero-shot super-resolution).

  • How does the discrete Fourier transform and weight truncation in FNO relate mathematically to evaluating a continuous Green's function integral?

docs.title: Efficient Training, Inference & AI Engineering
docs.text:
What this page solves

Turn algorithms into systems that are reproducible, measurable and deployable. This is your home ground: embedded and edge-deployment experience carries over directly to resource budgets, profiling and quantization; fill GPU training and inference runtimes as real gaps appear. P0: engineering and reproducibility required; P1: compression and performance.

docs.title: Knowledge map
docs.text: Level Topic What to understand P0 Engineering and reproducibility Data versions, random seeds, configs, dependencies, checkpoints, experiment logs P1 Performance and training efficiency Profiling, mixed precision, batch size, gradient accumulation, data loading and memory P1 Model compression Quantization, distillation, pruning and sparsity; verify quality and real speed separately P2 Large-model systems Efficient attention, KV cache, batching, parallelism and communication P2 Deployment and lifecycle ONNX and runtimes, edge devices, monitoring, drift, regression evaluation

docs.title: Core mechanics
docs.text:
Reproducibility: fix random seeds; record code version, dependencies, config and data version. Without these, "one hyperparameter change made it better" cannot be confirmed.

Profiling: measure before optimising. Separate data loading, forward, backward and optimiser step; GPU timing needs synchronisation, and the first iterations are warm-up and excluded. Many training runs are actually bottlenecked by data loading.

Mixed precision: forward and backward in FP16 / BF16 with FP32 master weights. BF16 has FP32's exponent bits, rarely overflows, and is preferred on modern GPUs; FP16 needs loss scaling.

Quantization: move weights (and activations) from float to INT8 or lower, shrinking the model and bandwidth needs. Post-training quantization (PTQ) sets scales with calibration data; quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates quantization error during training. Per-channel is more accurate than per-tensor.

Distillation: a small model imitates a large model's soft outputs (probability distributions), which carry more information than hard labels.

Pruning: remove unimportant weights. Unstructured pruning compresses a lot but is hard for hardware to accelerate; structured pruning (removing channels, attention heads) is what actually speeds things up.

Compute-bound vs memory-bound: whether an operator is fast depends on arithmetic intensity (operations per byte read). Many layers are bandwidth-bound, so fewer FLOPs need not mean lower latency — the same lesson as optimising kernels on an MCU.

Deployment: export to ONNX, then let runtimes such as TensorRT or ONNX Runtime fuse operators and quantize; on device also check peak memory, operator support and power.

docs.title: Follow-along · AI-6 · An explainable performance experiment
docs.text:
1. Reuse a model already running from F1, AI-2 or F4; no new task.
  2. Fix device, input and precision; separate loading, warm-up, forward and data processing.
  3. Time with proper device synchronisation, repeat, and record the latency distribution and peak memory.
  4. Change only batch, precision or one optimisation, then recheck quality and real resources.

Done when: the report states environment, measurement scope, repetitions and quality limits; theoretical FLOPs or parameter count are not deployment latency.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
What is wrong with timing a GPU forward pass with time.time()?

GPUs execute asynchronously; without synchronisation you time only the submission. Call torch.cuda.synchronize() first and exclude warm-up iterations.

BF16 or FP16?

BF16 has FP32's dynamic range, trains stably and needs no loss scaling — prefer it when hardware supports it; FP16 has more mantissa bits but overflows easily and needs loss scaling.

Pruning 50% of weights unstructured — why might inference not get faster?

Sparse weights are still stored and computed as dense matrices unless the hardware or runtime supports a specific sparse format; structured pruning reduces compute directly.

docs.title: Core mechanistic intuition · Soft routing & tensor flow
docs.text:
• Intuition: Self-attention is fundamentally content-based dynamic weighted information retrieval (soft routing). Each token projects a Query (what information am I seeking?) and a Key (what features do I contain?), computing attention affinities via inner products to aggregate Values (what information payload do I carry?).
  • Minimal tensor pipeline:
    • Input embedding: \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times D}\)
    • Linear projections: \(Q = X W_Q,\; K = X W_K,\; V = X W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times D}\)
    • Attention map: \(A = \text{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times T}\) (explicit all-to-all dependency graph)
    • Value aggregation & output projection: \(O = A V W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times D}\)
  • Trade-offs: Capturing unrestricted global dependencies requires \(O(T^2)\) pairwise interactions. In autoregressive inference, the memory bottleneck shifts from compute to KV Cache memory footprint and memory bandwidth limits.

docs.title: Check yourself · Critical thinking
docs.text:
• What is the mathematical purpose of the scaling factor \(\sqrt{d_k}\)? What happens to the Softmax gradient when \(d_k\) is large without scaling?
  • How does a causal mask operate at the matrix arithmetic level, and why is an architectural mask necessary rather than relying solely on the loss function?
  • Why does Pre-LN (normalizing before the sub-layer) offer significantly smoother gradient flow in deep networks compared to original Post-LN?

Revisit papers and historical bookmarks after implementing the small model.

docs.title: Embodiment & Space
docs.text:
What this page solves

Where the robot is and how it can move. Frames, rotations and forward/inverse kinematics are the shared language of perception, planning, control and policy learning — get one frame wrong and every downstream module is wrong. Required; prerequisite: linear algebra (matrix products, orthogonal matrices).

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Body, joints, position, orientation, frames You can mark the base, end-effector and camera frames on a robot drawing Foundation Homogeneous transforms, rotation representations, FK / IK E2 two-link example done; explain reachable vs unreachable targets Advanced Jacobians, singularities, dynamics Derive and implement for a chosen manipulation or mobile task

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Rigid poses and SE(3): an object's pose relative to a frame is a rotation R (3×3 orthogonal, determinant 1) plus a translation t, packed into a 4×4 homogeneous matrix T. Questions like "where is the object the camera sees, in the robot base frame?" are chains of T: T_base_obj = T_base_cam · T_cam_obj.

Rotation representations: matrices are explicit but have 9 numbers and must stay orthogonal; Euler angles have 3 numbers but suffer gimbal lock and wrap-around jumps; quaternions have no singularity and interpolate smoothly, with q and −q the same rotation; axis-angle says "how much about which axis". In practice: quaternions for storage and interpolation, matrices for computation, a continuous 6D representation for network regression.

Forward and inverse kinematics: FK maps joint angles to the end-effector pose — unique and easy. IK maps a desired pose back to joint angles — it may have no solution (out of reach), several (elbow up / down), or be numerically unstable near singularities.

Jacobian: maps joint velocities to end-effector velocities. Where J loses rank the robot is singular: some end-effector motion is impossible whatever the joints do. Velocity control, force control and numerical IK all depend on it.

Dynamics: how forces and torques produce accelerations (M(q)q̈ + C(q,q̇)q̇ + g(q) = τ). Not needed for kinematic simulation; needed for force control, fast motion and legged robots.

Embodiments: arms (manipulation), mobile bases (navigation), legged and humanoid (terrain and generality), dexterous hands (fine manipulation). The body decides degrees of freedom, available sensors and which algorithms apply.

docs.title: Debate · general humanoids vs. specialised bodies
docs.text: The humanoid camp argues the world is built for humans, so one general body reuses all human data and tools; the specialised camp argues a wheeled base plus an arm beats a humanoid on cost, reliability and energy, and most factory and warehouse tasks need no legs. Both coexist: research and capital chase humanoids, deployments are mostly specialised.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
How are T_cam_obj and T_obj_cam related, and how do you get one from the other?

They are inverses. The inverse has rotation Rᵀ and translation −Rᵀt; no general 4×4 inversion needed.

Why are Euler angles poor for interpolation or network regression?

Gimbal lock loses a degree of freedom in some poses, and angles jump at ±180°, giving unnatural interpolation and discontinuous losses.

Why can IK have several solutions or none?

None: the target is outside the workspace. Several: different joint combinations reach the same pose (elbow up / down). Near singularities the Jacobian loses rank and numerical solvers diverge.

Why check frames before algorithms when debugging a robot?

Wrong axis directions, units (m / mm, rad / deg) or transform order look like "the algorithm does not converge", but no algorithm change fixes them. One end-to-end check with a known pose is fastest.

docs.text:
How this page differs from the systematic track

The systematic track (overview, roadmap, E0–E5) starts from control and policy learning and builds full robotics knowledge week by week. This page is the smallest robot-perception loop you can close in two weeks: frames and cameras, ROS 2 basics, a 6DoF pose project wired into ROS 2, and one hands-on run of imitation learning. About 2–3 hours a day.

docs.title: Must-know interview questions (answer key)
docs.text: Question Key points Rotation representations and their pitfalls? Matrix (9 numbers, orthogonality constraint), Euler angles (gimbal lock, discontinuities), quaternions (no singularity, must normalise, q ≡ −q), axis-angle; networks often regress a continuous 6D representation Intrinsics vs extrinsics? Intrinsics: focal length and principal point, camera frame → pixels. Extrinsics: camera pose relative to the world or robot; hand–eye calibration finds camera-to-arm extrinsics Assumptions and limits of ICP? Needs a good initial guess or it falls into local minima; sensitive to outliers and partial overlap; point-to-plane converges faster; symmetric objects have multiple solutions Pose from 2D–3D correspondences? PnP (e.g. EPnP) + RANSAC for outliers, then non-linear refinement ADD vs ADD-S? ADD averages distances between corresponding points; symmetric objects use ADD-S (closest-point distance) so symmetry-equivalent poses are not marked wrong What matters in sensor fusion? Extrinsic calibration, time synchronisation, each sensor's noise model; a Kalman filter weights prediction and measurement by covariance Why does behaviour cloning fail in closed loop? Compounding errors drive the robot into states the demonstrations never covered (distribution shift); DAgger, wider data coverage, action chunking (ACT) help Common sim-to-real methods? Domain randomisation, system identification to shrink the gap, fine-tuning on real data; hardware-in-the-loop before the real robot What is a VLA? A vision-language model with an action head, trained on robot data; the hard parts are action representation, data scale and closed-loop evaluation tf tree and QoS in ROS 2? The tf tree keeps time-varying transforms between frames; QoS sets reliability, history depth etc., sensor streams usually use best-effort

docs.title: Embodied Intelligence · Overview
docs.text:
Understand the system first

Learn why each component exists and how components work together. Use videos, diagrams and lightweight simulation before detailed derivations and training.

docs.title: Robotics and embodied intelligence
docs.text:
Robotics studies sensing, motion and physical interaction. Embodied intelligence studies agents completing tasks through a body interacting with an environment. Robots are an important platform; learned policies are one family of methods.

Component Question Example Body, kinematics and dynamics What can move, how do joints relate to the end effector, and how do forces affect motion? Arm workspace Perception What is present and where is the target? Detect objects on a table State estimation What state explains incomplete, noisy observations? Fuse encoders and IMU Planning Which states or actions should be followed? Obstacle-avoiding path Control How should execution be corrected using feedback? Adjust velocity toward a target Policy Which action follows from observation, state or goal? Joint targets or end-effector displacement Software and simulation How are components connected and experiments repeated? ROS 2 messages, frames and replay Evaluation and deployment When does the task succeed or fail? Success, collision, timeout and latency 
flowchart LR
    A[Task or language instruction] --> B[Goals and skills]
    C[Sensor observations] --> D[Perception and state estimation]
    D --> E[Planner or learned policy]
    B --> E
    E --> F[Controller and actuators]
    F --> G[Body and environment]
    G --> C

This diagram explains responsibilities. Real systems can combine components and mix learned and classical methods.

docs.title: How learning methods relate
docs.text: Method Source of behavior First-pass lesson Classical planning and control Models, objectives, constraints and control laws A feedback baseline Imitation / behavior cloning Expert observation-action demonstrations Coverage gaps can cause closed-loop failures Reinforcement learning Interaction and rewards Reward design, exploration and training cost matter VLA Pretrained vision-language capabilities and robot action data Understand modalities, action representation and adaptation World model Environment observations, states and actions Prediction is distinct from a policy and task success

docs.title: Primary course and later practice
docs.text:
Role Selected resource Fit Scope Robot motion backbone Modern Robotics, textbook, videos and code Builds on your linear algebra, geometry and systems experience with consistent notation Preview and chapter introductions first; selected chapters 2–6 next; planning/control as needed Later robot-learning practice LeRobot tutorial Concepts, data, training and execution share an ecosystem Concepts first; E3 after PyTorch and action-interface checks; VLA training later

Selection evidence: Modern Robotics is required by UIUC ECE470 and appears in robotics community learning discussions. Its mathematical depth fits an engineering background; its emphasis is motion/control, with vision and learning studied later.

LeRobot is a newer official practice ecosystem with evolving tools. It is selected for workflow continuity, not presented as a decades-established course. Record versions and allow environment-debugging time.

Use official ROS 2 tutorials only for E1 software practice, and one PythonRobotics example for E2; neither is an additional full course to complete.

docs.title: Exploration E0: dissect a task
docs.text:
Choose navigation to a point or an arm picking an object. Watch a demonstration and identify:

  1. Body, sensors and available actions.
  2. Differences between goals, observations and estimated state.
  3. Which component chooses actions and which executes them.
  4. Success, failure, timeout and recovery definitions.

Completion: draw a feedback loop and distinguish localization, detection, planning, control and policy learning. Full SLAM or VLA training is not required.

docs.title: Later directions
docs.text:
Perception and estimation, planning and control, robot software, robot learning and edge deployment are possible specializations. Explore components on small tasks first, then select one body and task for deeper work.

Next: roadmap · Projects · Foundation overview

docs.title: Perception & State Estimation
docs.text:
What this page solves

What the robot sees, where it is, and where the target is. Perception turns raw sensor data into quantities you can plan and control with; state estimation fuses noisy, incomplete observations into trustworthy estimates. Required at entry level, depth by task: manipulation goes "detection → 6DoF pose → grasping", mobility goes "odometry → fusion → SLAM".

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Images, depth, point clouds, detection, pose, localisation and mapping You can say what observations mobile and grasping tasks each need Foundation Camera model, calibration, back-projection, filtering Derive pixel → 3D point; explain one Kalman step Advanced (manipulation) Detection / segmentation, registration, 6DoF pose, grasping P1 done with benchmark numbers Advanced (mobility) Visual / lidar odometry, multi-sensor fusion, SLAM Run an open-source odometry and evaluate trajectory error

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Camera model and calibration: the pinhole model projects camera coordinates to pixels with intrinsics K (focal lengths fx, fy, principal point cx, cy); distortion parameters undo lens bending. Extrinsics are the camera pose relative to the robot or world; hand–eye calibration finds the camera-to-arm extrinsics. Calibration error becomes pose error directly.

Depth and point clouds: RGB-D cameras, stereo or lidar give depth. Depth z plus pixel (u, v) back-projects through the intrinsics to a 3D point. Common point-cloud operations: voxel downsampling, normal estimation, outlier removal, plane segmentation.

Time synchronisation: sensors sample at different moments and must be aligned before fusion. A few tens of milliseconds of offset is centimetres of error on a moving robot.

Filtering and the Kalman family: each Kalman step predicts with a motion model and corrects with the observation, weighting them by covariance; the EKF linearises non-linear models, and the error-state Kalman filter (ESKF) is the usual form for IMU fusion. Particle filters represent arbitrary distributions with samples and suit multi-modal problems such as global localisation.

Odometry and SLAM: odometry estimates relative motion between frames and drifts; SLAM builds a map while localising and removes drift with loop closure and graph optimisation. Visual-inertial (VIO) and lidar-inertial (LIO) odometry are the mainstream today.

Object pose and affordances: a 6DoF pose is the object's rotation and translation relative to the camera — the precondition for grasping. Geometric methods (registration, PnP) are interpretable and need no training; learned methods (e.g. FoundationPose) are stronger under occlusion and symmetry. Affordances answer "where can it be grasped and how is it used".

3D scene representations: occupancy grids (navigation), point clouds and meshes (geometry), NeRF and 3D Gaussian splatting (photorealistic rendering), semantic maps (object-level understanding). The downstream task decides.

docs.title: Debate · explicit geometry vs. learned implicit representations
docs.text: Geometry: calibration, registration and optimisation are interpretable and verifiable, and you know why they fail. Learning: end-to-end networks are stronger under occlusion, weak texture and category generalisation, and foundation models handle new objects zero-shot. Industry is mostly hybrid: learning gives the initial guess or semantics, geometry refines and verifies.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Given pixel (u, v) and depth z, how do you get the 3D point in the camera frame?

x = (u − cx)·z / fx, y = (v − cy)·z / fy, z unchanged.

What happens if the observation noise covariance in a Kalman filter is set very large?

The filter trusts the prediction and nearly ignores observations: smooth but slow to respond. Very small makes it follow the observations closely and noisily.

Why does odometry drift, and how does SLAM fix it?

Small relative-motion errors accumulate. SLAM recognises revisited places (loop closure) and spreads the accumulated error over the whole trajectory with graph optimisation.

What is special about pose estimation for symmetric objects (e.g. a can)?

Rotations about the symmetry axis are indistinguishable from appearance, so several poses are equivalent; evaluate with ADD-S and train with symmetry-aware losses, or the network learns an average.

docs.title: Planning & Control
docs.text:
What this page solves

Planning answers "which route and which trajectory"; control answers "how to correct errors while executing". This is the most classical, interpretable part of robotics and the baseline learned policies are compared against. Required at entry level; your feedback-control and system-identification background transfers directly.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Paths vs trajectories, planning vs control, open vs closed loop Explain "choosing a route" vs "correcting execution error" Foundation A*, PID and trajectory tracking E1 and one E2 experiment done, with failures reported Advanced Sampling planners, trajectory optimisation, MPC, force / impedance control, whole-body control Go deep on one, chosen by body and task

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Paths and trajectories: a path is a geometric sequence of points; a trajectory adds time (velocity, acceleration). Planners usually find a collision-free path first, then time-parameterise it within velocity and acceleration limits.

Search-based planning: A* finds shortest paths on grids or graphs and is optimal if the heuristic never overestimates. Great for 2D navigation; the state space explodes in high dimensions.

Sampling-based planning: RRT and PRM sample the continuous space and connect samples into a tree or graph — suited to high-dimensional arm configuration spaces; RRT* is asymptotically optimal. Results need smoothing.

Trajectory optimisation: treat the trajectory as decision variables, minimise a cost (time, energy, smoothness) under constraints (collision, joint limits). CHOMP and TrajOpt are typical; sensitive to initialisation.

Feedback control: PID acts on the error, its integral and its rate — the most common baseline. Trajectory tracking = feed-forward (from the desired trajectory) + feedback (correcting deviation).

Model predictive control (MPC): each cycle, predict ahead with a model, solve a constrained optimisation online, execute only the first step, re-solve next cycle. Handles constraints explicitly at a computational cost; used widely in legged robots and autonomous driving.

Force and impedance control: contact tasks (peg-in-hole, wiping) cannot be position-controlled alone. Impedance control makes the end-effector behave like a spring-damper, compliant on contact instead of pushing hard.

Whole-body control: humanoids and legged robots must satisfy balance, contacts and several task goals at once, often as a prioritised quadratic programme.

docs.title: Debate · model-driven vs. learning-driven
docs.text: Model-driven (planning + MPC) is interpretable, enforces safety constraints and needs little data, but requires accurate models and struggles with complex contact and perception uncertainty. Learning-driven (imitation, RL) captures behaviours that are hard to model, but needs lots of data and fails opaquely. The trend is layering: learning decides what to do, model-based controllers do it safely.

docs.text:

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why must the A* heuristic not overestimate?

Overestimating can make the search abandon the truly optimal path early, losing the optimality guarantee; an admissible heuristic guarantees the shortest path.

Why do arm planners use RRT rather than A*?

Arm configuration spaces are 6–7 dimensional; gridding them explodes exponentially, while sampling never discretises the whole space.

Advantages and costs of MPC over PID?

Advantages: explicit constraints, prediction with a model, multivariable coordination. Costs: needs a model and an optimisation every cycle, heavy computation and tight real-time demands.

Why do contact tasks need impedance control?

Pure position control turns small position errors into large contact forces that can damage the part or the robot; impedance control makes force proportional to deviation, so contact is compliant.

docs.title: Learned Policies
docs.text:
What this page solves

Teach a robot to act from data: a policy maps observations to actions. It can imitate demonstrations, be reinforced by rewards, or generalise through a pretrained vision-language model. Advanced, required: prerequisites are a PyTorch training loop and the notions of observation and action.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Policies, behaviour cloning, imitation, RL, VLA You can say where each method's learning signal comes from Foundation Demonstrations, action representations, ACT, closed-loop evaluation E3 done; demonstration coverage compared against success rate Advanced Diffusion policies, RL, VLA and cross-embodiment adaptation Two methods compared on one fixed task

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Behaviour cloning (BC): treat demonstrations as supervised data and regress actions. Simple and effective, but with compounding error: small mistakes push the robot into states the demonstrations never covered, where the policy is worse, and errors grow. This is why "low offline loss, closed-loop failure" happens.

Fighting distribution shift: DAgger asks the expert to label states the policy actually visits; wider data coverage (perturbations, varied initial states); action chunking (predicting a short sequence at once) reduces the number of decisions.

ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers): predicts the next k actions at once, encoding images and joint states with a Transformer and smoothing execution with temporal ensembling. Data-efficient; a common baseline for bimanual manipulation.

Diffusion policies: generate action sequences with a diffusion model and can represent multi-modal distributions (several valid actions in one state, e.g. going around an obstacle left or right); BC with mean-squared error averages the modes into a wrong action.

Reinforcement learning (RL): maximise cumulative reward through interaction. Suited to tasks with clear rewards and abundant simulation (legged locomotion, in-hand rotation); hard parts are reward design, exploration and sample efficiency, so training usually happens in simulation and transfers.

VLA (vision-language-action models): add an action output to a pretrained vision-language model and train on large robot datasets (OpenVLA, π0, SmolVLA). Strength: language instructions and cross-task generalisation. Hard parts: action representation (discrete tokens or continuous generation), data scale and inference latency.

Hierarchical policies: a high level (language model or planner) chooses sub-goals or skills; a low level (learned policy or classical controller) executes at high frequency. The most deployed structure today.

Data sources: teleoperation (high quality, expensive), cross-embodiment datasets (e.g. Open X-Embodiment), human videos (abundant but without action labels), simulation. Data often matters more than the algorithm.

docs.title: Debate · modular vs. end-to-end · imitation vs. reinforcement
docs.text: End-to-end: one large model from pixels to actions learns behaviours nobody could design, and scale will bring generalisation. Modular: only interpretable, debuggable, separately verifiable modules reach production. Imitation depends on demonstration quality and coverage; RL depends on rewards and simulation fidelity. The common recipe is imitation for an initial policy, then RL or online data to fine-tune.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why can behaviour cloning have low training loss but fail in closed loop?

Compounding error causes distribution shift: execution errors lead to states the data never covered, where the policy never learned, and errors grow. Offline loss only measures demonstration states.

Why are multi-modal action distributions a problem for MSE regression?

If one state allows two valid actions (go left, go right), MSE learns their average — straight into the obstacle. Diffusion policies or mixture outputs can represent several modes.

Why does action chunking help?

Predicting several steps at once means fewer decisions and fewer chances for compounding error, and actions are more coherent over time.

Why is VLA inference latency a deployment bottleneck?

One large-model forward pass can take tens to hundreds of milliseconds while control runs at tens to hundreds of hertz. Common fix: a low-frequency large model outputs action chunks or sub-goals, a high-frequency small controller executes.
