docs.title: Hands-on · RGB-D 6DoF Object Pose Estimation
docs.text:
In one sentence

Given an RGB-D frame and a 3D model of an object, recover the object's rotation and translation in the camera frame — the question a robot must answer before it can grasp. This project goes from a public benchmark to an edge device and ends with a real iPhone capture.

Code: Pose6D-Edge

docs.title: Where it sits in the map
docs.text:
It is the first complete project of the "manipulation: detection, 6DoF pose and grasping" elective in Perception & State Estimation, and the P2 level (depth, point clouds, pose) of Vision & 3D Space. Unlike E0–E5, which start from control and policies, this project starts from perception and lines up directly with industrial robot perception roles (detection, 6DoF pose, 3D reconstruction, grasping, plus model quantisation for deployment).

RGB ──► instance segmentation (YOLO-seg, or SAM from a box) ──► object mask
                                                                   │
Depth ─► back-projection with camera intrinsics ◄──────────────────┘
          │
          ▼
   FPFH + RANSAC global registration ─► multi-scale point-to-plane ICP (+ 180° flips)
          │
          ▼
   rank hypotheses by render consistency (z-buffer silhouette + depth) ─► pose (R, t)
          │
          ▼
   video: ICP tracking from the previous pose, re-initialised from SAM when the score drops

docs.title: What to learn first (in project order)
docs.text:
# Topic Why now One resource Self-check 1 Pinhole camera, intrinsics, back-projection The only way from a depth image to a point cloud Open3D RGBD tutorial; the model section of the OpenCV calibration docs Derive (u, v, z) → (x, y, z) by hand 2 Rigid transforms SE(3), rotation representations A pose is an SE(3); evaluation, flips and tracking are all compositions Modern Robotics ch. 3.1–3.3 Explain T_cam_obj vs T_obj_cam 3 Registration: ICP (point-to-point / point-to-plane), FPFH + RANSAC The geometric core; ICP's dependence on initialisation is a classic interview question Open3D ICP and global registration; Cyrill Stachniss' ICP lecture Why ICP falls into local minima; why symmetric objects flip 4 Pose metrics: ADD / ADD-S, BOP No evaluation, no claim BOP benchmark challenge description Why symmetric objects use ADD-S 5 Fine-tuning instance segmentation, synthetic data Replacing GT masks with learned ones makes it a full system Ultralytics Segment docs; CS231n detection & segmentation lecture Why train on PBR renders and never on the test split 6 TensorRT FP16 / INT8 and latency measurement A common plus in industry roles and an existing strength Ultralytics export docs; NVIDIA TensorRT INT8 calibration guide Report latency and accuracy before and after quantisation 7 Landscape of learned pose estimators Know where the geometric baseline stops FoundationPose (CVPR 2024), MegaPose, GDR-Net method figures Where learned methods win under occlusion and symmetry

What transfers

System identification and state estimation map directly onto "registration = solving for the best rigid transform" and "tracking = using the previous state as a prior". TinyAuton's quantisation and kernel work maps onto step 6.

docs.title: Ten-day plan
docs.text: Day Task Done when 1 Set up, download LM-O, run eval_pose.py with GT masks; read geometry.py and registration.py GT-mask result in the README reproduced 2–3 Download LM PBR renders, convert with prepare_yolo.py, train YOLO-seg on the desktop GPU Validation mask mAP and training curves 4 eval_pose.py --masks yolo for the full system GT-mask vs learned-mask rows side by side 5–6 Export TensorRT FP16 / INT8 on the Jetson, run bench_latency.py, re-evaluate accuracy Latency and accuracy table 7–8 Scan an object with the iPhone, record RGB-D with Stray Scanner, run iphone_demo.py A video and GIF with the pose overlay 9–10 Polish the README, push to GitHub, record a short walkthrough Results table and GIF on the repo front page

docs.title: Results so far (measured on a cloud CPU)
docs.text:
Setting ADD(-S) < 0.1d All 1,445 LM-O targets, GT masks 0.643 (median error 7.6° / 8.6 mm) Same 150 targets, hypotheses ranked by point fit only 0.52 Same 150 targets, + 180° flip hypotheses and render-consistency ranking 0.62 Same 20 targets, box-prompted SAM masks (mean IoU 0.75) 0.55 One tracking step from a 5° / 10 mm perturbation 0.85

Failures are mostly 180° flips of near-symmetric objects seen from one side, and heavily occluded instances (visible fraction below 30 %). That is exactly where learned methods such as FoundationPose are strong; this project is a transparent geometric baseline with an edge-deployment path, not a state-of-the-art claim.

docs.title: Record keeping
docs.text:
Follow the common record rules of the embodied projects: versions, data sources, a fixed evaluation set, success rates with failure examples, and your own changes. Report offline metrics, dataset results and real captures separately.

Back to guided projects · Perception & State Estimation

docs.title: Embodied Intelligence · Guided Projects
docs.text:
Explore systems before learning policies

E0–E2 build intuition; E3 connects data, training and execution. E4–E5 are electives. Follow upstream installation/code for your selected version; use the learning steps and acceptance criteria below.

Project Prerequisite Environment Depth E0 · Task dissection Introductory concepts Browser, videos or demos Orientation E1 · ROS 2 turtlesim Python and terminal basics Supported ROS 2 system, CPU Fundamentals E2 · Small algorithms Python, frames and arrays CPU Fundamentals E3 · Simulated imitation F1-equivalent PyTorch and observation/action semantics Graphics; GPU or tutorial training notebook Intermediate entry E4 · Language and action E3 and a fixed body/task Skill-calling or VLA-dependent Elective E5 · Deployment and transfer Working, evaluated policy Target hardware and interfaces Elective P1 · 6DoF pose estimation (hands-on) Camera model, rigid transforms, PyTorch basics RGB-D dataset or a LiDAR iPhone; GPU training, Jetson deployment Perception track

docs.title: Dissect a robot task
docs.text:
Follow: Modern Robotics Preview/chapter introductions; consult the selected LeRobot tutorial for learning concepts.

Choose point navigation or manipulation. Identify the body, sensors, goal, observations, state, actions and success conditions; draw the feedback loop.

Acceptance: a one-page system explanation distinguishing perception, planning, control and policies.

docs.title: Turtlesim: messages and feedback
docs.text:
Primary: ROS 2 Tutorials, Beginner CLI Tools (turtlesim, nodes, topics), then Client Libraries (Python publisher/subscriber). Match the distribution; FishROS is an optional Chinese explanation aid.

  1. Run the original example, use keyboard control and inspect messages.
  2. Publish velocity and identify units and frequency.
  3. Subscribe to pose; log goal distance and heading error.
  4. Turn toward the goal, then use simple proportional feedback; slow near the goal.
  5. Add tolerance, velocity limits, timeout and stopping on missing pose messages.
  6. Repeat from several initial positions and save trajectories/logs.

Personal change: replace fixed velocity with position feedback.

Acceptance: at least five starting points, endpoint errors and timeouts, plus an explanation of open-loop commands vs. feedback. Turtlesim demonstrates software and planar control, not physical robot dynamics or manipulation.

docs.title: Planning or arm motion: choose one first
docs.text:
Follow: PythonRobotics / documentation, a collection of visual algorithm examples.

Route Example Experiment Mobile robot A* grid search Vary goals, obstacles and robot radius; measure feasibility, path length and runtime Arm Two-link example under Arm Navigation Vary link lengths and targets; compare joints/endpoints and unreachable goals
  1. Run the original and identify inputs, outputs, units and frames.
  2. Change one condition at a time; save animations and results.
  3. Create and explain a failure.

Acceptance: three conditions and one failure analysis. Explore both routes if useful; choose one body/task for a substantial project.

docs.title: Learn actions from simulated demonstrations
docs.text:
Follow: LeRobot imitation learning in simulation / GitHub, with ACT concepts.

Check the environment first

The simulation tutorial is on main. Match source and dependencies and record the commit. Verify graphics and keyboard/gamepad interaction first. Use CPU for initial environment/data checks; arrange GPU or the linked notebook for training. Allow installation/debugging time at this later stage.

  1. Teleoperate the original task using keyboard or gamepad.
  2. Record and inspect alignment of images, state, actions and time.
  3. Reserve evaluation data by complete episode, not randomly mixed neighboring frames.
  4. Train ACT; save configurations, curves and checkpoints.
  5. Define success, failure, timeout and termination before autonomous execution.
  6. Run at least 20 fixed evaluations; report successes/attempts, initial conditions and failure types.
  7. Change demonstration count or coverage and compare under the same evaluation conditions.

Personal change: design a data-coverage experiment and explain cases with low training loss but failed execution.

Acceptance: data documentation, versions, training logs, videos, success rate and failures. Report offline action errors separately from task success; simulation results do not establish hardware performance.

docs.title: Connect language: choose one route
docs.text:
Route Reference Sequence Acceptance Skill calling Applications & agents, existing E1/E3 interface Bounded skills/arguments → rule baseline → model output → validation and feedback Normal, ambiguous and unsupported instructions; separate interpretation and execution success VLA adaptation SmolVLA Check robot/compute/data support → collect or convert → fine-tune → fixed evaluation Document data and action interfaces; test changed task conditions

SmolVLA involves robot configuration and data; arbitrary E3 data is not automatically compatible. Check cameras, states, actions, annotations and controllers. If resources are limited, complete skill calling or study the VLA architecture first.

Both routes require closed-loop validation; a VLA is not necessarily a separate high-level planner.

docs.title: Edge deployment and sim-to-real
docs.text:
References: keep the E3 environment in Simulation & sim-to-real and consult the selected robot's interfaces. Add platforms only after defining the transfer problem.

Fix the model/task. Measure software-loop latency, then connect target hardware in the loop. Check frames, units, control frequency, action limits and stopping. Validate gradually on hardware under controlled conditions and record domain gaps/recovery.

Acceptance: latency, resources, task success and transfer comparisons. Distinguish software-in-the-loop, hardware-in-the-loop and physical robot experiments; simulation alone does not complete transfer.

docs.title: Common record
docs.text:
Keep tutorial, versions, run instructions, task definitions, data sources, results, failures and personal changes. Label future work as planned and report only measured outcomes.

Roadmap

docs.title: Embodied Intelligence · Roadmap
docs.text:
Short on time?

Do the two-week Get Started first: it enters through perception and covers frames, ROS 2, P1 · 6DoF pose and one imitation-learning run; if you pick the perception branch in round two, continue from P1.

Use Modern Robotics as the backbone, then LeRobot for robot learning. Build on your geometry, signals and engineering background; fill specific spatial/interface gaps rather than restart mathematics and programming. Estimates assume 8–10 hours weekly; ROS 2 documentation and examples serve projects, not extra full courses.

docs.title: First pass: orientation and a small feedback loop
docs.text:
Stage Estimate Minimum knowledge Tutorial and project Completion 0 · Overview and spatial basics 1–2 weeks Body, observations, state, frames and feedback Modern Robotics introduction and selected chapters 2–3; Overview, E0 Explain the loop, frames and actions 1 · Software exploration 2–3 weeks Basic Linux, nodes, messages, position and velocity ROS 2 official tutorials; E1 Subscribe to pose and publish feedback velocity commands 2 · Algorithm intuition 1–2 weeks Frames, kinematics, paths and errors PythonRobotics; E2 Use the two-link arm with Modern Robotics chapters 4–6; A* is an alternative 3 · Data and policies 3–5 weeks PyTorch, demonstrations, observation/action interfaces and success rates LeRobot imitation in simulation; E3 Go from data to a trained policy and repeated closed-loop evaluation

Complete foundation F1 before policy training, or verify that you can read a PyTorch training loop. Initial simulations can use ground-truth state without a full visual SLAM system.

docs.title: Second pass: deepen one task
docs.text:
Branch Focus Project extension Perception and estimation Calibration, detection, pose and fusion, chosen for the task Replace ground truth with sensor estimates and measure errors Planning and control Tracking, constraints and stability; MPC/force control as needed Compare controllers under disturbances and delay Software and systems ROS 2, replay, interfaces, latency and recovery Make the task reproducible and debuggable Learned policies Imitation, data coverage, action representations, RL/VLA E4: adapt and evaluate a language-conditioned policy Deployment and sim-to-real Identification, domain gaps, runtimes and resources E5: hardware-in-the-loop, then gradual robot validation

Choose one small example first, then one body and task for a substantial project. Legged/humanoid robots, dexterous hands, whole-body control, full SLAM and world models are electives.

docs.title: Three foundation-model connections
docs.text:
Route Output interface Evaluate LLM skill selection Goals or skill names and parameters Instruction understanding, interface constraints, feedback and recovery VLA policy Actions or action sequences Adaptation data, timing, control interfaces and success World-model-assisted decisions Predicted states, observations or latent features Prediction errors, planning benefit and distribution shifts

Choose one route at a time. Adding an action head alone does not establish a usable robot policy.

docs.title: Project records
docs.text:
• Versions: tutorial date, OS, dependencies, simulator, code commit and model/data revisions.
  • Task: observation/action semantics, control frequency, success, timeout and termination.
  • Evaluation: fixed initial states or seeds, successes/attempts, failure types and latency.
  • Contribution: what changed, why, observed results and limitations.

After E1–E3, use target roles to select a branch for a complete project.

E0–E5 project steps · Software and simulation

docs.title: Simulation & Sim-to-Real
docs.text:
What this page solves

Success in simulation is not success on the robot. This page covers narrowing the gap between simulation and reality, deploying on constrained hardware, and validating in stages. Advanced: go deep once E3 reproduces reliably; your digital-twin-to-field work (adaptive triggering) and edge deployment experience apply directly.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Simulation, software-in-the-loop, hardware-in-the-loop, real robot You can say what each kind of experiment validates Foundation Fixed evaluation conditions, control rate, latency E3 repeated with offline error and closed-loop success reported separately Advanced Domain randomisation, system identification, edge deployment, safety and recovery E5 before/after comparison with the domain gap reported

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
The reality gap: simulation and reality differ in dynamics (friction, mass, delay), sensing (lighting, noise, camera parameters) and actuation (motor response, backlash); policies exploit loopholes that only exist in simulation.

Domain randomisation: randomise friction, mass, lighting, textures, camera pose and more during training so reality looks like one more sample. Simple and effective; costs are more conservative policies and longer training.

System identification: estimate simulator parameters from real data so the simulation behaves like the robot. Complements randomisation: identify first to shrink the gap, then randomise around the identified values. It is the same kind of problem as your structural modal identification.

Differentiable simulation: gradients through the simulator let you fit real trajectories or optimise policies directly; gradients are unreliable across contact discontinuities.

Staged validation: software-in-the-loop (algorithm + simulation) → hardware-in-the-loop (real controller / compute + simulation) → controlled real robot → open environment. Change one factor per stage so failures can be attributed.

Real-time and resource budgets: control rate, end-to-end latency, compute and power together bound model size. Quantisation, distillation and kernel optimisation decide whether a policy runs on time on the onboard computer.

Safety and failure handling: action limits, speed limits, emergency stop, watchdog timeouts, a safe posture after detected anomalies — all in place before the real robot.

Why evaluation is hard: real trials are slow, initial conditions are hard to reproduce and environments change. Fix a set of initial states, record every failure type, and report "successes / trials" rather than a bare percentage.

docs.title: Debate · real data vs. simulated data
docs.text: Real-data camp: simulation is never real enough; teleoperated real data is most reliable and scale will bring the cost down. Simulation camp: only simulation provides the data volume and safety RL needs, and rendering and physics keep improving. In practice locomotion leans on simulation + RL, fine manipulation on real demonstrations, and mixed training is becoming the norm.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
What happens if the randomisation range is too wide?

The policy must work in every extreme, becomes overly conservative, performs worse and trains less easily. Cover the real parameter uncertainty, not as much as possible.

How do system identification and domain randomisation relate?

They complement each other: identification pulls simulator parameters to the real centre, randomisation covers the remaining uncertainty; identify first, then randomise around it.

What does hardware-in-the-loop validate, and what not?

It validates latency, compute and interfaces on the real computer; not real physical interaction (contact, friction) or real sensor noise.

Why report successes / trials on the real robot instead of one success rate?

Real trials are few; 16 of 20 and 160 of 200 carry different confidence. Also report initial conditions and failure types.

docs.title: Robot Software & Simulation
docs.text:
What this page solves

Connect observation, algorithms and actuation into a system you can run, debug and reproduce. Almost every industry robotics role asks for ROS 2; simulation decides whether you can iterate without a real robot. Required; prerequisites: Python, basic Linux.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation What nodes, messages, frames and simulators are for You can draw the node graph of one robot task Foundation ROS 2 pub/sub, tf2, rosbag, RViz E1 done; your frames display correctly in RViz Advanced Simulator interfaces, latency and real time, integration You can tell "no data", "wrong frame" and "interface mismatch" apart from logs

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Nodes and communication: ROS 2 splits a system into nodes. Topics are continuous streams (camera images); services are request/response ("reset"); actions are long tasks with feedback ("move to a point"). Choosing the wrong one is a common design error.

QoS: sets reliability (reliable / best-effort), history depth and durability. Sensor streams usually use best-effort — dropping a frame beats blocking; commands and maps use reliable. Incompatible publisher and subscriber QoS fails silently.

tf2 and the frame tree: keeps every time-varying transform between frames. Asking "where is this camera point in the map frame at time t" multiplies along the tree and interpolates in time. Wrong timestamps are the top cause of broken fusion.

URDF: XML describing links, joints, inertia and visuals; the shared input to RViz, kinematics solvers and simulators.

rosbag record and replay: record sensor data once, then debug algorithms on identical inputs, separating sensing problems from algorithm problems.

Simulators: MuJoCo (accurate contact dynamics, good for manipulation and learning), Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab (GPU-parallel, realistic rendering, large-scale training and synthetic data), Gazebo (tight ROS integration, mobile robots). Pick one, by task.

docs.title: Debate · ROS 2 vs. in-house middleware
docs.text: ROS 2 has a large ecosystem and is what job ads name, but carries learning and performance overhead; many production teams (autonomous driving, consumer robots) build lean middleware to control latency and dependencies. The concepts — nodes, messages, tf, record/replay — transfer either way.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Should camera images use a topic, a service or an action? Why?

A topic: images are a continuous stream that needs no per-message acknowledgement; a service would block the sender and an action makes no sense.

A subscriber never receives data although the topic is listed. Most likely cause?

Incompatible QoS (e.g. best-effort publisher, reliable subscriber), a mismatched message type, or a wrong namespace.

A tf lookup raises an extrapolation error while fusing two sensors. What does it mean?

The requested timestamp is outside the time range of the available transforms — usually unsynchronised timestamps or a transform published too rarely.

Why record a rosbag before debugging?

With fixed input every algorithm change is compared on the same data, results are reproducible, and you can tell sensor problems from algorithm problems.

docs.title: Applications & Agents
docs.text:
What this page solves

Turning a model into a system that solves real problems: connect your own documents (retrieval augmentation), connect tools (agents), and prove it works (evaluation). Required practice: much day-to-day LLM work in industry lives here.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Prompts, context, RAG, tool calls, agents One QA flow with retrieval and a tool drawn Foundation Chunking, embeddings, retrieval, source display, test sets F2 done; retrieval and generation failures told apart Advanced Agent loops, structured output, multi-step planning, automated evaluation One read-only tool added to F2 and evaluated

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Prompt and context engineering: the model only sees its context. System prompts set role and rules, few-shot examples set format, relevant material sets the source of facts. Longer context costs more and dilutes attention.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): chunk documents, embed and index them; at question time retrieve the most relevant chunks into the context and answer from them. Knowledge stays updatable and answers traceable.

Chunking and retrieval quality: chunks too large add noise, too small lose context; hybrid retrieval (BM25 keywords + vectors) and rerankers improve recall markedly. Most RAG problems are retrieval problems, not generation problems.

Tool calling: the model emits a structured call (name + arguments), the program executes it and returns the result. The model executes nothing itself; permissions and safety live in the program.

Agents: a "think → call tool → observe → continue" loop until the task is done. Powerful but brittle: more steps, more accumulated error; limit steps and validate each output.

Structured output: ask for JSON matching a schema, or use constrained decoding to guarantee the format, so downstream code parses reliably.

Evaluation: a fixed question set (including unanswerable and adversarial ones), human or model grading, statistics by failure type. Without a test set every "improvement" is a feeling.

docs.title: Debate · long context vs. retrieval
docs.text: Long context: windows reach a million tokens, so put everything in — simpler, nothing missed. Retrieval: cheaper, faster, traceable, and information in the middle of long contexts gets overlooked. In practice both: retrieve to narrow down, then use a long-enough context for the relevant material.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
A RAG answer is wrong. How do you tell retrieval from generation?

Check whether the retrieved chunks contain the answer: if not, it is retrieval (chunking, embeddings, top-k); if yes but wrong, it is generation (prompt, model, context too long).

Why include questions the documents cannot answer?

To test whether the model admits it does not know instead of inventing an answer — the most common hallucination scenario.

Why do agents get less reliable with more steps?

Each step has some error rate and errors propagate; ten steps at 95% each gives about 60% overall.

Where is the safety boundary of tool calling?

The model only requests calls; the program executes them, validates arguments, enforces permissions and requires human confirmation for side effects.

docs.title: Architecture & Representation
docs.text:
What this page solves

What is inside a large model: how text becomes vectors, how attention lets tokens look at each other, and how blocks stack into a GPT. With this page, training, inference and multimodality share one skeleton. Required; prerequisites: matrix products, PyTorch tensors.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Tokens, embeddings, context, attention, generation Input-to-output drawn; F0 done Foundation Residuals, normalisation, positions, the training loop Small GPT built in F4; every tensor shape explained Advanced Long context, MoE, state-space models, linear attention A comparison experiment designed for one question

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Tokenisation: BPE and similar algorithms split text into sub-word units. Vocabulary size sets the embedding size and sequence length; how Chinese, code and numbers are split affects cost and capability (digits split badly make arithmetic harder).

Embeddings: each token looks up a vector; the output layer maps vectors back to vocabulary probabilities. Many models tie input embeddings and output weights.

Self-attention: each token produces Q, K, V; softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V lets each position gather information from others by content similarity. A causal mask keeps generation from seeing the future. Multiple heads attend to different relations.

Transformer block: attention + feed-forward network (FFN, most of the parameters), each wrapped in a residual connection and normalisation. Modern LLMs use pre-norm (RMSNorm) and SwiGLU for stabler training.

Positional encoding: attention itself is order-blind. Absolute encodings add a vector per position; RoPE rotates Q and K by position so attention depends only on relative distance — today's default.

Long context: attention is O(n²) and the KV cache grows linearly. Remedies: sliding windows, sparse attention, FlashAttention (same complexity, far less memory traffic), RoPE extrapolation and interpolation.

Mixture of experts (MoE): replace the FFN with many experts and let a router activate a few per token. Large total parameters, little compute per token; hard parts are load balancing and memory (all experts must fit).

Alternatives: state-space models (Mamba) and linear attention compress history into a fixed-size state, O(1) per inference step and cheaper on long sequences, but weaker at exact long-range recall; hybrids are spreading.

Unified multimodal representation: images become patches, audio becomes frames, encoders turn them into tokens of the same width as text, and everything enters one Transformer.

docs.title: Debate · autoregressive vs. diffusion
docs.text: Autoregressive generation, token by token, is simple to train and natural for language — the LLM default. Diffusion denoises in parallel and dominates images, video and robot actions; diffusion language models are explored for parallel decoding. The trade-off is the simplicity of sequential generation against the efficiency and multi-modality of parallel generation.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why divide attention scores by √d?

The variance of Q·K grows with d; large values push softmax towards one-hot and kill gradients. Dividing by √d keeps the variance near 1.

How is the causal mask implemented?

Set the upper triangle (future positions) of the score matrix to −∞ before softmax so their weights become 0.

Where are most parameters in a Transformer block?

In the FFN: two linear layers with an inner width around 4× the hidden size (SwiGLU ≈ 8/3× with three matrices) — about twice the attention projections.

Why is MoE large in parameters but cheap at inference? And memory?

Each token visits only a few experts, so compute follows active parameters; but all expert weights must be loaded, so memory follows total parameters.

docs.title: Must-know interview questions (answer key)
docs.text: Question Key points What are Q, K and V? Three linear projections of each token; Q·K decides what to attend to, the weights mix V; divide by √d to keep softmax from saturating Why does a KV cache speed things up? Past tokens' K and V do not change during decoding, so cache them and compute only the new token; memory grows linearly with length Prefill vs decode? Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel, compute-bound, sets time-to-first-token; decode generates one token at a time, memory-bandwidth-bound, sets tokens/s What is RoPE? Rotary position embedding: rotate Q and K by position so their dot product depends only on relative position; extrapolates better What do pretraining, SFT and preference optimisation each change? Pretraining learns language and knowledge; SFT learns instruction format and behaviour; RLHF / DPO shift outputs toward human preferences How does LoRA work? Freeze W, learn a low-rank update ΔW = BA (rank r ≪ dimension); few trainable parameters, can be merged back; alpha / r scales it Common quantisation methods? Mostly weight-only (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF k-quants); activations are harder because of outliers; 4-bit usually costs acceptable quality How do you locate a RAG failure? Check whether retrieved chunks contain the answer: if not, it is retrieval (chunking, embeddings, top-k); if yes but wrong, it is generation (prompt, model) How do you evaluate hallucination? A fixed question set including unanswerable ones; check whether each claim is supported by a source; count unsupported claims Is a longer context always better? Cost and latency grow with length and attention dilutes; retrieval plus a curated context usually beats filling the window

docs.title: Inference & Deployment
docs.text:
What this page solves

Once a model is trained, how to make it fast, small and still good on given hardware. This is your home ground: quantisation and memory work on MCUs carries over to LLMs, only at a different scale. Basics required, depth by direction; prerequisite: you can load and run a pretrained model.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Prefill vs decode, time-to-first-token, throughput, memory You can explain why TTFT and generation speed differ Foundation Measuring under fixed conditions, quantisation comparison F5 done with quality, latency and memory reported together Advanced KV-cache management, continuous batching, speculative decoding, kernels A bottleneck located by measurement, gains and limits explained

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Two phases: prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel, mostly compute-bound, and sets time-to-first-token (TTFT); decode generates one token at a time, reads all weights every step, is mostly memory-bandwidth-bound, and sets tokens/s.

Back-of-envelope decode speed: at batch 1, tokens/s ≲ memory bandwidth ÷ weight bytes. A 7B model in FP16 is ~14 GB, so on 100 GB/s the ceiling is ~7 tokens/s; at 4-bit, ~3.5 GB and ~28 tokens/s. That is why quantisation speeds things up.

KV cache: caches past tokens' K and V to avoid recomputation; size = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × length × batch × bytes. With long contexts or many users it outgrows the weights. GQA / MQA share KV heads to shrink it; PagedAttention removes fragmentation.

Decoding strategies: greedy, temperature sampling, top-k, top-p (nucleus), beam search. Higher temperature means more diversity and more errors; low for factual tasks, high for creative ones.

Quantisation: weight-only quantisation (GPTQ, AWQ, GGUF k-quants) is most common and 4-bit usually costs acceptable quality; weight-and-activation quantisation (e.g. W8A8) is harder because activations have outliers — SmoothQuant moves the difficulty from activations to weights.

Distillation and pruning: distillation trains a small model on a large model's outputs; pruning removes unimportant weights or structures (only structured pruning truly speeds up).

Speculative decoding: a small draft model guesses several tokens, the large model verifies them in one parallel pass and accepts the correct prefix; the output distribution is exactly the large model's, and speed depends on acceptance rate.

Continuous batching and serving: servers batch requests at token granularity to keep the GPU busy; vLLM, TensorRT-LLM and SGLang are typical.

Edge runtimes: llama.cpp (CPU / GPU / Apple Silicon, GGUF), ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, MLC-LLM. At the edge, peak memory, power and TTFT matter most.

docs.title: Debate · general acceleration vs. hardware-specific optimisation
docs.text: General: rely on mature frameworks and the GPU ecosystem, build once, deploy anywhere. Specific: operator fusion and custom quantisation for an NPU or chip win orders of magnitude in power and cost, at a high porting cost. Edge and automotive increasingly go specific — where an embedded background pays off.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why does total decode throughput rise with batch size?

Batch-1 decode is bandwidth-bound: one read of the weights yields one token. Larger batches serve more tokens per read and raise compute utilisation until compute becomes the limit.

A 7B model at 4-bit on a 50 GB/s device: roughly what batch-1 decode speed?

About 3.5 GB of weights, so a ceiling of ~50 / 3.5 ≈ 14 tokens/s; real numbers are lower.

Does speculative decoding change output quality?

No. Rejection sampling keeps the output distribution identical to the large model's; only speed changes.

Why is activation quantisation harder than weight quantisation?

Activations change with the input and some channels have huge outliers, so one scale leaves most values with too little precision.

docs.title: Multimodality & Action Interfaces
docs.text:
What this page solves

How models see images and hear sound, and how they go from describing to acting: how vision-language models (VLMs) connect to robot actions (VLAs). This is where foundation models meet embodied intelligence. Introduction required, VLA adaptation elective.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Image–text alignment, VLM, VLA inputs and outputs You can state the difference between a VLM and a VLA Foundation Run a VLM, probe spatial and counting ability F3 done with at least three error types recorded Advanced Action representations, robot data adaptation, closed-loop evaluation One route of embodied E4 done

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Contrastive image–text alignment (CLIP): an image encoder and a text encoder map matching pairs into one space, pulling matches together and pushing mismatches apart. Result: zero-shot classification and retrieval, and the vision encoder of many VLMs.

VLM structure: a vision encoder (ViT) turns the image into patch vectors, a projection maps them into the language model's embedding space, and they enter the LLM as "image tokens" alongside text.

VLM limits: good at description and common-sense QA, often wrong on exact counting, fine spatial relations, metric quantities (distance, size) and 3D reasoning. Verify spatial outputs separately before using them on a robot.

From VLM to VLA: add an action output and train on robot data (image + instruction + action). Actions can be discretised into tokens generated like words (RT-2, OpenVLA) or produced by a continuous head (diffusion or flow matching, e.g. π0) as smooth action chunks.

Action representations: joint angles or end-effector pose, absolute or delta, single step or chunk. The choice decides cross-robot data reuse and control smoothness.

Cross-embodiment and data: robots differ in joints, camera placement and control rate. Datasets like Open X-Embodiment train across bodies, but adapting to your robot still needs its own data.

Two ways to connect a robot: an LLM chooses skills and parameters for existing controllers (interpretable, easy to verify), or a VLA outputs actions directly (more generalisation potential, harder to debug).

docs.title: Debate · discrete action tokens vs. continuous action generation
docs.text: Discrete: treat actions as vocabulary tokens and reuse language-model training and inference unchanged. Continuous: discretisation loses precision; high-frequency fine manipulation needs smooth continuous chunks. High-performing VLAs are moving to continuous heads; discrete is the simplest to implement.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
How does CLIP differ from a VLM?

CLIP only maps images and text into one space for matching and cannot generate text; a VLM feeds image features into a language model and answers open questions about the image.

Why can't a VLM's "the cup is left of the plate" drive a grasp directly?

The description is qualitative, may be wrong and gives no metric pose; grasping needs millimetre-level 3D position and orientation from, or verified by, geometric perception.

Why do VLAs often predict action chunks instead of single steps?

Large-model inference is slow; single-step prediction cannot keep up with control rates, while a chunk covers several control cycles per inference and is more coherent.

What does using an LLM as a skill selector buy you?

Actions run on verified controllers, so they stay safe and controllable; the language model only interprets instructions and composes skills, and failures are easy to locate.

docs.text: Concept Meaning Example ML / deep learning Learn parameters from data; deep learning uses multilayer neural networks Image classification Foundation model A broadly pretrained model adaptable to multiple tasks Language or vision adaptation LLM A language-sequence model; common generative LLMs predict successive tokens Answers, summaries and code Token / embedding A discrete processing unit / its numeric vector representation English vs. Chinese tokenization Transformer An architecture using attention and other sequence-processing components Context-dependent representations Pretraining / fine-tuning Learn broad capabilities / adapt parameters using task data SFT or LoRA on domain examples RAG Retrieve material and include it in context Website Q&A with sources Tool calling / agent Execute interfaces / organize models, tools and task steps Query records, then call a plotting tool VLM / VLA Vision-language processing / its connection to robot actions Image Q&A / manipulation World model Predict environment dynamics under actions Compare potential outcomes

docs.title: Training and use
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Offline data] --> B[Pretraining and adaptation]
    B --> C[Model weights]
    D[User input] --> E[Tokens and context]
    F[Retrieved material or tool results] --> E
    C --> G[Inference]
    E --> G
    G --> H[Answer or tool request]

Training updates parameters; inference uses them. RAG supplies external material; tools execute programs. Understand these roles before combining them.

docs.title: Primary overview: Hung-yi Lee's GenAI introduction
docs.text:
Follow one introductory course: the official course page provides Chinese lectures, slides and assignments. Start with lecture 1, then 6–10 for training, agents and Transformers, and 12 for evaluation. Revisit other lectures as needed.

Fit: your mathematics, signal-processing and engineering experience provide a base; the immediate gap is the model-domain vocabulary and system picture. Use the 2024 edition consistently for concepts and current official documentation for software details.

Optional intuition aid: if attention remains unclear, watch 3Blue1Brown's visual Transformer explanation. This supplements one concept rather than adding another full introductory course.

docs.title: Next primary course: Karpathy's implementation path
docs.text:
Use Neural Networks: Zero to Hero to connect concepts to code. Check PyTorch first, watch micrograd if needed, then the first two makemore lectures and the GPT implementation. Do not jump directly into the GPT video.

The author specifies Python programming and introductory mathematics as prerequisites. Your engineering background helps; assess PyTorch through practice. Community learning advice also places it after introductory study. Difficulty here follows the author's prerequisites rather than popularity alone.

Two backbone courses only. Use HF documentation when loading or adapting models. If you prefer text, Raschka's book and code can replace the Karpathy implementation track; choose one rather than study both.

  2. Compare a bare question, a question with reference material, and a request for evidence.

  4. Sketch a document assistant and label data, retrieval, model, tools and evaluation.

docs.title: Project · Quantizing a Small Language Model: from RTN to GPTQ / AWQ
docs.text:
What this project solves

You already do FP8 / int8 quantization on MCUs; this project moves the same skill to large models. On a 0.5B model, compare several quantization algorithms on accuracy, memory and speed by hand, and explain where the accuracy loss comes from. It fills the gap between "tuning llama.cpp flags" and "understanding quantization algorithms". One NVIDIA GPU with 8 GB+ memory is enough; about 5–7 days.

docs.title: How this differs from F5
docs.text: F5 · Inference comparison This project Focus Runtime: how fast each quantized build runs Algorithms: why each method works or fails Where quantization comes from Pre-converted GGUF files Your own calibration and quantization Deliverable Speed and memory table Accuracy–memory–speed comparison + per-layer error analysis

docs.title: Target level
docs.text: Skill After the project you can Quantization basics Explain symmetric / asymmetric, per-tensor / per-channel / group-wise, W8A8 vs W4A16 Post-training quantization (PTQ) Quantize once each with RTN, GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant and say what each fixes Error analysis Find the most sensitive layers; explain why activation outliers make activation quantization hard Inference Measure prefill and per-token decode speed; know what KV-cache quantization saves Quantization-aware training (QAT, optional) Compare PTQ and QAT on a small task

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Baseline: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct in FP16. Fixed evaluation: WikiText-2 perplexity + one small task (e.g. ARC-Easy or a HellaSwag subset in lm-evaluation-harness) + a manual check on 20 fixed prompts. Record memory, prefill and decode speed.
  2. Plain rounding (RTN): write a few dozen lines yourself to quantize linear-layer weights per channel and per group (group size 128) to INT8 and INT4, dequantize, and evaluate. No library — the point is to see where the error comes from.
  3. GPTQ and AWQ: W4A16 with llm-compressor, 128 calibration samples. Compare perplexity and task score, then swap the calibration set for text from another domain and watch what changes.
  4. Activation quantization and SmoothQuant: W8A8 first without smoothing, then with SmoothQuant. Plot per-channel activation maxima for a few layers to see the outlier channels.
  5. Per-layer sensitivity: quantize one layer at a time (others FP16), record the perplexity change and plot sensitivity; keep the most sensitive layers in FP16 and try mixed precision.
  6. Speed: serve two quantized results with vLLM (and once on a Jetson if available); measure prefill, decode and memory; then enable FP8 / INT8 KV cache and see the memory saved at long context.
  7. Optional · QAT: fine-tune with torchao's QAT flow on a small downstream task; compare INT4 PTQ with QAT.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• One summary table: method × bit width → perplexity, task score, memory, prefill / decode speed.
  • Two plots: activation outlier channels, per-layer sensitivity.
  • A short "accuracy-drop debugging" note: which layer is most sensitive, why, and how to fix it.
  • Code repository and README with model version, calibration set, hardware and repetitions; mark unfinished parts as "planned".

docs.title: Curated resources
docs.text:
• Main tool · llm-compressor

    vLLM's quantization library with ready examples for GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant and FP8; results load directly in vLLM.

    Open repository

  • QAT and low-bit · torchao

    PyTorch's quantization and sparsity library, with INT4 / INT8 weight quantization and a QAT flow.

    Open repository

  • Evaluation · lm-evaluation-harness

    One harness for perplexity and common benchmarks, so before and after use the same ruler.

    Open repository

Three must-read papers (method section and main figures only):

  • GPTQ

    Column-by-column quantization with second-order error compensation.

    arXiv 2210.17323

  • AWQ

    Protects salient weight channels found from activation magnitude.

    arXiv 2306.00978

  • SmoothQuant

    Migrates activation outliers into the weights so W8A8 becomes feasible.

    arXiv 2211.10438

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why do LLMs usually use weight-only quantization (W4A16) instead of quantizing weights and activations?

LLM activations contain a few channels with very large values (outliers); per-tensor quantization starves the other channels of precision. Decode is mostly memory-bandwidth bound, so compressing weights alone captures most of the speed gain.

What fundamentally separates GPTQ from RTN?

RTN rounds each weight independently; after quantizing a column, GPTQ uses a Hessian approximation to spread that column's error onto columns not yet quantized, reducing overall output error.

Why do results change when the calibration set comes from another domain?

GPTQ, AWQ and SmoothQuant all rely on activation statistics from calibration data; if that distribution differs from real use, the chosen salient channels and scales are off.

What does KV-cache quantization mainly save?

At long context and large batch the KV cache can exceed the weights in memory; quantizing it mainly saves memory and enlarges usable context and batch, with little effect on single short-prompt speed.

docs.title: Tokens, context and limits
docs.text:
Follow: HF LLM Course chapter 1, then chapter 2 tokenization.

  1. Compare tokenization and counts for English and Chinese equivalents.
  2. Give a fixed question partial, complete and irrelevant reference material.
  3. Include questions unsupported by the material.
  4. Record questions, context, answers, model and date.

Personal change: vary only context and compare outcomes.

Acceptance: a results table and diagram explaining tokenization, context, generation and retrieval.

docs.title: PyTorch image classifier
docs.text:
Diagnostic: if you can explain validation/gradient updates and independently save/load a model, proceed to F4. Otherwise study only gaps exposed by Quickstart.

Follow: Learn the Basics, using FashionMNIST and the tutorial notebooks.

  1. Run Quickstart to see the full workflow.
  2. Study tensors, DataLoader, models, autograd and optimization.
  3. Save and reload the model in a separate inference script.
  4. Change learning rate or width while holding other factors fixed.
  5. Split validation data from training data for selection; use the test set for final reporting. Inspect wrong predictions.

Personal change: compare two configurations and explain overfitting or undertraining.

Acceptance: code, dependencies, training/validation curves, test results and error analysis. F1 also prepares you for robot policies.

docs.title: Personal website document assistant
docs.text:
Follow: LlamaIndex official starter / GitHub. Build the minimum document-Q&A workflow; its default cloud models require API setup and usage costs.

  1. Run the original example and record tutorial/dependency versions.
  2. Select 5–10 personal Markdown files and inspect parsing and chunks.
  3. Build the index; inspect retrieved passages before generated answers.
  4. Display source files/passages and handle absent information.
  5. Create at least 20 questions: direct facts, cross-passage synthesis and unanswerable questions, with expected evidence.
  6. Compare direct answers and RAG. Tune one chunking or retrieval setting, then evaluate on reserved examples.

Personal change: use your material, expose sources and build fixed evaluations.

Acceptance: runnable app, diagram, question set, support checks and failures; distinguish retrieval and generation failures.

Next: improve retrieval/evaluation in the same codebase; see Applications for a tool extension rather than start another RAG course.

docs.title: Vision-language capabilities and limits
docs.text:
Follow: HF image-text-to-text. Match development documentation to source, or choose the corresponding stable page.

  1. Run one original image Q&A example.
  2. Use 10 fixed images for object, counting, spatial and task-related questions.
  3. Keep prompts, outputs and human checks, including at least three failure types.
  4. Change one prompt or input-size setting and compare quality and inference time.

Acceptance: successful and failed examples explaining what remains between image Q&A and reliable actions. Continue to robot E3–E4 for action learning.

docs.title: Small GPT and one adaptation task
docs.text:
Primary: Karpathy Zero to Hero / companion code. Micrograd if gradients are unclear, then the first two makemore lectures, followed by the GPT video/code. Use small models/data rather than target a general assistant.

Text alternative: LLMs-from-scratch, chapters 2–5, can replace this track. The full narrative is in its book; choose one implementation. Later use chapter 6 or 7, or HF's fine-tuning reference, for adaptation.

Personal change: vary context length, training data or width. Pretraining and adaptation may use different model sizes; a toy model need not become a general chatbot.

Acceptance: architecture, curves, held-out examples, limitations and tensor-shape explanations. Continue to training for LoRA/SFT practice as needed.

docs.title: Inference on a fixed task
docs.text:
Follow: llama.cpp README and run instructions, with the inference topic.

Run a supported small model, then compare quantizations of the same base model. Fix hardware, prompts, output length and settings; measure time to first token, generation speed, peak memory and answer quality. Repeat measurements and separate loading from inference.

Acceptance: configurations, results, quality regressions and bottleneck analysis. Document limitations when models or hardware differ.

docs.title: Common record
docs.text:
Keep tutorial links, date, commit, dependencies, model/data revisions, run instructions, results and personal changes. Label tutorial reproductions, personal experiments and independent projects accurately; planned work is not completed work.

docs.text:

docs.title: Training & Adaptation
docs.text:
What this page solves

The stages that take a large model from "read a lot" to "follows instructions and preferences", and what you can do with limited compute (usually adaptation, not pretraining from scratch). Concepts required, practice up to LoRA; prerequisites: F1's training loop and data splits.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Pretraining, SFT, preference optimisation, parameter-efficient tuning You can say what each stage changes in the model Foundation Splits, hyper-parameters, checkpoints, LoRA One small-model LoRA fine-tune evaluated on held-out examples Advanced Scaling laws, parallel training, preference optimisation, RL with verifiable rewards One question explored in depth

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Pretraining objective: next-token prediction (cross-entropy) on vast text. Most knowledge and capability — and most cost — come from here.

Scaling laws: loss falls as a power law in parameters, data and compute. Chinchilla: for a fixed compute budget scale parameters and data together (~20 tokens per parameter); small models today are often "over-trained" to make inference cheaper.

Data: deduplication, quality filtering and mixture (web, code, maths, languages) often matter more than architecture changes. Benchmark contamination inflates metrics.

Distributed training: data parallel (a copy per GPU, split data), tensor parallel (split matrices), pipeline parallel (split layers); ZeRO / FSDP shard optimiser states, gradients and parameters across GPUs to save memory.

Instruction tuning (SFT): train on instruction–response pairs so the model learns the chat format and to follow instructions; loss only on the response.

Preference optimisation: RLHF trains a reward model then optimises with PPO; DPO trains directly on "better vs worse" pairs, with no separate reward model or RL loop — simpler and more stable.

RL with verifiable rewards: for maths and code, where correctness can be checked automatically, use it as the reward (e.g. GRPO); the main source of recent reasoning gains.

Parameter-efficient tuning: LoRA freezes W and trains a low-rank update ΔW = BA, usually under 1% of parameters; QLoRA quantises the base to 4-bit and trains LoRA on top, so billion-parameter models fit on one GPU.

docs.title: Debate · keep scaling vs. new methods
docs.text: Scaling: more data and compute remain the most reliable source of progress. Methods: better data, synthetic data, RL and test-time compute (thinking longer at inference) deliver similar gains more cheaply. The recent trend combines both: pretraining scale slows while post-training and inference-time compute grow.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
Why compute SFT loss only on the response?

The instruction is given input the model need not learn to generate; including it wastes capacity and encourages parroting prompts.

What if LoRA rank r is too small or too large?

Too small: not expressive enough. Too large: more parameters, more overfitting, diminishing returns. 8–64 is common, with alpha scaling.

What does DPO remove compared with RLHF?

The separately trained reward model and the PPO loop; it applies a classification-style loss directly to preference pairs — more stable and cheaper.

Why are small models trained far beyond the Chinchilla-optimal token count?

Chinchilla optimises training compute only; inference cost accumulates with every call, so a smaller model trained on more data is cheaper overall.

docs.title: World Models
docs.text:
What this page solves

A world model predicts "if I do this, what will the environment become". It can be used to plan in imagination, generate data for policy learning, or capture physical regularities in video. Advanced elective; your Manifold Dynamics research (a learned latent state + transition operator) is structurally a world model.

docs.title: How far to go
docs.text: Level Learn Done when Orientation Prediction, state, action conditioning, planning You can distinguish world models, policies and video generators Foundation Latent dynamics models, planning in the model You can follow one latent world model's training and use Advanced Training policies with world models; prediction vs task benefit An experiment that separates "predicts well" from "decides well"

docs.title: Core knowledge
docs.text:
Definition: given the current state (or observation history) and an action, predict the next state or observation: s_{t+1} = f(s_t, a_t). A video predictor without action input can only watch, not decide.

Latent modelling: predicting pixels is expensive and full of irrelevant detail. The mainstream encodes observations into a compact latent state and learns dynamics there (e.g. Dreamer's RSSM), decoding only when needed.

Planning in the model: simulate the outcomes of candidate action sequences and execute the best (the MPC idea), or train a policy on imagined trajectories (Dreamer), cutting real interaction drastically.

Predictive representation learning (JEPA): predict the representation of masked or future parts instead of reconstructing pixels, learning more abstract and robust states — usable as a world-model encoder.

Video generation as a world simulator: large video generators show some physical common sense and are used to synthesise robot training data or long-horizon predictions; physical consistency and action controllability remain unreliable.

Compounding error and evaluation: multi-step prediction errors accumulate. Judge a world model not only by one-step error but by whether policies planned or trained with it do better in the real environment.

docs.title: Debate · generating pixels vs. predicting representations
docs.text: Generation: realistically generating future video demonstrates understanding and yields training data directly. Representation (e.g. LeCun's JEPA): reconstructing every pixel is wasteful and unnecessary; intelligence needs prediction over abstract states. Both are advancing; the final criterion is the benefit to downstream decisions.

docs.title: Self-check
docs.text:
How does a video predictor differ from a world model?

A world model is conditioned on actions and answers "what if I do a"; an unconditioned video predictor only says "what usually happens next" and cannot support decisions.

Why model dynamics in a latent space rather than pixels?

Pixels are high-dimensional and full of task-irrelevant detail (texture, lighting), making prediction hard and slow; a latent space is compact and keeps what matters for dynamics.

Why can planning be poor even when one-step error is low?

Errors accumulate over rollouts, and the policy actively seeks regions where the model is wrong but predicts high return (model exploitation).

What do Manifold Dynamics and Dreamer share, and how do they differ?

Both learn a latent state and a transition operator. Manifold Dynamics detects anomalies as deviation from the learned flow and is not action-conditioned; Dreamer is action-conditioned and trains a policy.

docs.title: 1.1 Brief introduction to SHM
docs.text: Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) aims at safety assessment, life prediction, and maintenance optimization of in-service structures. Sensors are deployed on structures to continuously collect vibration and response data, which are then combined with models and algorithms to identify and monitor the structural condition and potential damage.

docs.title: 1.2 Basic models in structural dynamics
docs.text:
For an \(n\)-degree-of-freedom structure, the matrix form is

\[ \mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{x}}(t) + \mathbf{C}\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) + \mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{f}(t) \tag{1} \]

Notation:

  • \(\mathbf{x}(t),\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t),\ddot{\mathbf{x}}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^n\): displacement, velocity, acceleration;
  • \(\mathbf{M},\mathbf{C},\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\): mass, damping, stiffness matrices;
  • \(\mathbf{f}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^n\): external force;
  • \(n\): number of degrees of freedom.

Modal frequencies, damping ratios, and mode shapes are determined by these matrices and are key quantities for system and modal identification.

docs.title: 1.3 State-space models
docs.text:
A linear time-invariant system can be written in state-space form. In continuous time,

\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}}(t) = \mathbf{A}_c \mathbf{x}(t) + \mathbf{B}_c \mathbf{u}(t) \tag{2} \] \[ \mathbf{y}(t) = \mathbf{C}_c \mathbf{x}(t) + \mathbf{D}_c \mathbf{u}(t) \tag{3} \]

Continuous-time (2)(3) notation:

  • \(\mathbf{x}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^n\): state vector;
  • \(\mathbf{u}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^m\): input vector;
  • \(\mathbf{y}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^p\): output vector;
  • \(\mathbf{A}_c,\mathbf{B}_c,\mathbf{C}_c,\mathbf{D}_c\): continuous-time state, input, output, and feedthrough matrices;
  • \(n,m,p\): dimensions of state, input, and output.

The discrete-time form \((k \in \mathbb{Z})\) is

\[ \mathbf{x}[k] = \mathbf{A}_d \mathbf{x}[k-1] + \mathbf{B}_d \mathbf{u}[k] \tag{4} \] \[ \mathbf{y}[k] = \mathbf{C}_d \mathbf{x}[k] + \mathbf{D}_d \mathbf{u}[k] \tag{5} \]

Discrete-time (4)(5) notation:

  • \(\mathbf{x}[k],\mathbf{u}[k],\mathbf{y}[k]\): state, input, and output at step \(k\);
  • \(\mathbf{A}_d,\mathbf{B}_d,\mathbf{C}_d,\mathbf{D}_d\): discrete-time system matrices (from discretization);
  • \(k\): discrete time index.

Figure 1: Block-diagram representation of a state-space model.

In SHM, displacement and velocity are collected into a structural state \(\mathbf{z}(t) = [\mathbf{x}(t)^\top,\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)^\top]^\top\); in discrete time the parameterized form is

\[ \mathbf{z}[k] = \mathbf{A}(\theta)\,\mathbf{z}[k-1] + \mathbf{B}(\theta)\,\mathbf{f}[k] \tag{6} \] \[ \mathbf{y}[k] = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{z}[k] + \mathbf{v}[k] \tag{7} \]

SHM parameterized form (6)(7) notation:

  • \(\mathbf{z}[k]\): structural state at step \(k\) (stack of displacement and velocity);
  • \(\theta = \{\mathbf{M},\mathbf{C},\mathbf{K}\}\): structural parameters (mass, damping, stiffness matrices);
  • \(\mathbf{A}(\theta),\mathbf{B}(\theta)\): state and input matrices depending on \(\theta\);
  • \(\mathbf{f}[k]\): external force at step \(k\);
  • \(\mathbf{H}\): observation matrix (sensor type and placement);
  • \(\mathbf{v}[k]\): measurement noise.

This compact model is the basis for system and modal identification in SHM.

The following figures illustrate the block-diagram representation of this state-space model, and its specialization for SHM with parameter vector \(\theta\) and measurement operator \(\mathbf{H}\):

Figure 2: State-space model for SHM with parameters and measurement operator.

docs.title: II. Common system/modal identification methods
docs.text: Below are core, classical methods worth prioritising; each is given a one-sentence summary of the main idea and a one-sentence note on typical use.

docs.title: 2.1 PP
docs.text:
• Name: Peak Picking (PP).
  • Main idea: Read dominant peaks in the response power spectrum or Fourier spectrum for natural frequencies and use multi-channel amplitude ratios to estimate mode shapes.
  • Typical use: Quick, preliminary modal estimates when modes are well separated, damping is low, and SNR is good.
  • Edge computing: Well suited. Pros: FFT and peak search only; very low compute and memory; easy to run in real time. Cons: Low accuracy and robustness; sensitive to noise and close modes.

docs.title: 2.2 ARX / ARMAX (PEM)
docs.text:
• Name: ARX / ARMAX with prediction-error methods (PEM).
  • Main idea: Describe input–output (or output-only) dynamics with difference-equation models (ARX/ARMAX, etc.) and estimate parameters by minimising one-step-ahead prediction error; modal parameters follow from the identified model.
  • Typical use: Parametric system identification when input–output data are available; AR/ARMA variants for output-only cases.
  • Edge computing: Moderately suited. Pros: Compact model, controllable data size; modest cost for low order. Cons: Sensitive to order choice; MLE iteration can be heavy; numerical stability depends on implementation.

docs.title: 2.3 FRF
docs.text:
• Name: FRF curve fitting (Frequency Response Function curve fitting); common implementations include the Rational Fraction Polynomial (RFP) form.
  • Main idea: Fit measured FRFs in the frequency domain with rational functions (or orthogonal polynomials); extract modal frequency, damping, and mode shape from poles and residues.
  • Typical use: Laboratory modal testing with known excitation (impact, shaker) when accurate modal parameters are required.
  • Edge computing: Partially suited. Pros: Fitting can be limited to a frequency band; reduced-order fit lowers cost. Cons: Needs known excitation and FRF estimation; rational fit and root finding are non-trivial; full-band multi-channel is resource-heavy.

docs.title: 2.4 Transfer function fitting
docs.text:
• Name: Transfer function fitting (TF fitting).
  • Main idea: Fit a rational transfer function (e.g. \(H(s)=N(s)/D(s)\) or polynomial ratio in frequency) to measured FRF or input–output frequency-domain data; extract modal frequency, damping, and mode shape from the poles and residues of the fitted model.
  • Typical use: When FRF or frequency-domain data are available (e.g. after impact or shaker test); complements FRF estimation by providing a parametric modal model; used in classical modal analysis.
  • Edge computing: Partially suited. Pros: Can restrict to a frequency band; reduced-order fit lowers cost. Cons: Needs FRF or frequency data; rational fitting and root finding often require iteration or nonlinear optimisation; multi-channel full-band is resource-heavy.

docs.title: 2.5 FDD / EFDD
docs.text:
• Name: Frequency Domain Decomposition / Enhanced FDD.
  • Main idea: Decompose the output power spectral density matrix via SVD; dominant singular vectors approximate mode shapes and peak singular value curves give frequencies; EFDD refines damping by single-mode fitting in frequency bands.
  • Typical use: Output-only operational modal analysis (e.g. bridges, buildings under ambient excitation).
  • Edge computing: Moderately suited. Pros: Output-only; SVD per frequency line can be done in batches; manageable when channels and lines are limited. Cons: Buffer needed for PSD; EFDD damping fit adds an extra step.

docs.title: 2.6 Random Decrement (RDT / RDM)
docs.text:
• Name: Random Decrement Technique / Random Decrement Method (RDT / RDM).
  • Main idea: From long output-only response under ambient excitation, extract many short time segments triggered by a condition (e.g. level crossing) and average them to cancel the random part of excitation, yielding a free-decay signature (impulse-like response) that can be used to estimate modal frequency and damping (and, with multiple channels, mode shapes).
  • Typical use: Output-only operational modal analysis when you want a clean free-decay signal from ambient data; commonly used as a preprocessing step for NExT/ERA or for simple damping estimation.
  • Edge computing: Moderately suited. Pros: Mostly buffering + triggering + averaging; no heavy optimization. Cons: Needs sufficient data for averaging; trigger choice affects quality; multi-channel processing increases memory and bandwidth.

docs.title: 2.7 ERA / NExT-ERA
docs.text:
• Name: Eigensystem Realization Algorithm / Natural Excitation Technique – ERA.
  • Main idea: ERA forms Markov parameters and a Hankel matrix from impulse or free-decay response, then uses SVD and minimal realisation to obtain a state-space model and modal parameters; NExT-ERA under ambient excitation builds equivalent impulse responses from output auto- and cross-correlations, then applies ERA to them.
  • Typical use: ERA when impulse or free-decay data are available; NExT-ERA for output-only operational modal analysis (e.g. bridges, buildings under ambient excitation).
  • Edge computing: Moderately suited. Pros: Output-only; Hankel size can be limited; single SVD per run, no iteration. Cons: Correlation estimation needs buffer; order selection and multi-order trials increase cost.

docs.title: 2.8 SSI
docs.text:
• Name: Stochastic subspace identification (SSI: SSI-COV / SSI-DATA).
  • Main idea: Build block Hankel/Toeplitz matrices from output (or input–output) data, obtain observability/controllability subspaces via SVD, then recover a discrete state-space model and modal parameters from its system matrix.
  • Typical use: Output-only or input–output; robust modal identification with long, multi-channel data; widely used in operational modal analysis.
  • Edge computing: Poorly suited. Pros: Best identification quality; industry standard. Cons: Large Hankel and SVD; multi-order stabilization diagram; high compute and memory; heavy for low-power edge; may need reduced setup or cloud–edge split to offload.

docs.title: 2.9 BAYOMA
docs.text:
• Name: Bayesian Operational Modal Analysis (BAYOMA).
  • Main idea: In output-only setting, treat modal parameters as random variables; use Bayesian inference (e.g. MCMC, variational or Laplace approximation) to estimate their posterior from response data, yielding parameter estimates and uncertainty (e.g. credible intervals).
  • Typical use: Output-only OMA when uncertainty quantification or confidence intervals for modal parameters are needed; complements point-estimate methods such as SSI and FDD.
  • Edge computing: Poorly suited. Pros: Provides posterior and uncertainty for risk and decision-making. Cons: Bayesian computation (MCMC etc.) is heavy; high compute and memory; typically offline or cloud.

docs.title: III. Damage assessment methods
docs.text: Methods below are ordered by dimension: detection first, then localisation, then quantification. Each entry is tagged with the dimension(s) it addresses (Detection / Localisation / Quantification).

docs.title: 3.1 Modal parameter change vs baseline
docs.text:
• Main idea: Compare current estimates of modal frequency, damping, or mode shape with a healthy baseline; form a scalar or vector index (e.g. frequency shift, damping change) and apply a threshold or simple statistical test to decide if damage is present.
  • Typical use: When a healthy baseline exists and a quick yes/no or “significant change” decision is needed.
  • Dimensions: Detection; can support rough quantification (e.g. magnitude of change).
  • Edge computing: Well suited. Pros: Comparison and threshold only; very low compute and memory. Cons: Depends on baseline quality; simple indices may miss damage.
  • Online/offline: Suited to online (real-time comparison).

docs.title: 3.2 Response- or feature-based anomaly detection
docs.text:
• Main idea: Use statistical features of multi-channel response (e.g. PCA residual, covariance change, Mahalanobis distance) or a novelty index; compare to the baseline distribution and flag anomaly when a threshold is exceeded, without explicit modal parameters.
  • Typical use: Many channels, data-driven setup, when accurate modal identification is not required.
  • Dimensions: Detection.
  • Edge computing: Moderately suited. Pros: Baseline/model can be trained offline; online step is projection and threshold only. Cons: Covariance or PCA cost grows with channel count.
  • Online/offline: Baseline offline, detection online; or fully offline.

docs.title: 3.3 MAC and mode-shape–based indices
docs.text:
• Main idea: Use Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC), mode shape difference, or mode slope to measure current vs baseline; regions or modes with large spatial change can indicate damage location.
  • Typical use: When multiple mode shapes are available and damage detection plus rough localisation is needed.
  • Dimensions: Detection, localisation.
  • Edge computing: Moderately suited. Pros: MAC etc. are inner products and norms; light compute. Cons: Needs current mode shapes; if online, depends on online modal ID.
  • Online/offline: Can be online (if modes are online) or offline.

docs.title: 3.4 Flexibility / stiffness matrix method
docs.text:
• Main idea: Flexibility and stiffness are inverses in the reduced DOF space; from identified modal parameters (frequency, mode shape, mass approximation) build the flexibility matrix or invert to get stiffness. Damage reduces stiffness and increases flexibility; compare current and baseline flexibility or stiffness (or their change) to find damage regions and to support quantification of stiffness loss.
  • Typical use: When several modes and mass approximation are available; common for beams and frames; can be expressed as flexibility or stiffness, same in essence.
  • Dimensions: Detection, localisation; can support quantification.
  • Edge computing: Partially suited. Pros: Clear physics; manageable when matrix size is small. Cons: Needs several modes and mass approximation; matrix build or inverse.
  • Online/offline: Often offline; can be online with light implementation.

docs.title: 3.5 Curvature and strain mode shape
docs.text:
• Main idea: Derive curvature (or strain mode) from displacement mode shape; damage causes local stiffness drop and a spike or discontinuity in curvature/strain, used to localise damage.
  • Typical use: Dense sensors, beam- or plate-like structures, when localisation is the goal.
  • Dimensions: Localisation.
  • Edge computing: Moderately suited. Pros: Curvature from mode difference or fit; modest compute; easy to distribute. Cons: Needs dense sensors and mode shape estimate.
  • Online/offline: Can be online (if modes online) or offline.

docs.title: 3.6 Model updating and stiffness inversion
docs.text:
• Main idea: Use a parameterised FE or reduced model (e.g. element stiffness reduction factors); fit or invert against current test data (modes, response) via optimisation or Bayesian inference to estimate stiffness loss and thus damage location and severity.
  • Typical use: When a reliable structural model exists and quantitative location and severity are required.
  • Dimensions: Detection, localisation, quantification.
  • Edge computing: Poorly suited. Pros: Quantitative. Cons: Optimisation/inversion is iterative and heavy; high compute and memory.
  • Online/offline: Suited to offline; online usually needs cloud or high-end node.

docs.title: Eigensystem Realization Algorithm (ERA) / NExT-ERA
docs.text: This page expands 2.7 ERA / NExT-ERA from the SHM roadmap: ERA builds Markov parameters and a Hankel matrix from impulse or free-decay response, then uses SVD and minimal realisation to obtain a state-space model and modal parameters; NExT-ERA under ambient excitation builds equivalent impulse responses from output auto- and cross-correlations, then applies ERA for output-only operational modal analysis.

docs.title: Concept
docs.text:
Core idea — ERA (Eigensystem Realization Algorithm) is a time-domain identification method: from impulse or free-decay sequences we form Markov parameters, assemble a Hankel matrix, perform SVD and truncation to get a minimal realisation, yielding a discrete state-space \((\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C})\); the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\) give continuous-time poles (natural frequency and damping ratio), and \(\mathbf{C}\) with eigenvectors give mode shapes. NExT (Natural Excitation Technique) states that under white or broadband ambient excitation, the cross-correlation of two response channels satisfies the same homogeneous differential equation as the impulse response, so we can estimate auto/cross-correlations from output-only data and use them as “equivalent impulse response” in ERA, i.e. NExT-ERA. In short: ERA is impulse/free decay → Markov → Hankel → SVD → state-space → modes; NExT-ERA is output-only → correlation estimate → equivalent impulse → ERA.

Principle (brief) — Discrete LTI state-space:

\[\mathbf{x}[k+1] = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}[k] + \mathbf{B} u[k], \qquad \mathbf{y}[k] = \mathbf{C} \mathbf{x}[k] + \mathbf{D} u[k]. \tag{1}\]

The pulse response (Markov parameters) are \(\mathbf{h}_0 = \mathbf{D}\), \(\mathbf{h}_k = \mathbf{C} \mathbf{A}^{k-1} \mathbf{B}\) (\(k \geq 1\)). Stacking \(\mathbf{h}_k\) into a Hankel matrix \(\mathbf{H}\) links its rank to observability/controllability; SVD of \(\mathbf{H}\) truncated to order \(n\) yields \(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{\Sigma},\mathbf{V}\) from which \(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}\) are recovered (minimal realisation). Eigenvalues \(\mu_i\) of \(\mathbf{A}\) are discrete poles; map to continuous time by \(\lambda_i = \ln(\mu_i)/\Delta t\) to get modal poles, hence \(\omega_r\), \(\zeta_r\) and mode shapes \(\mathbf{\phi}_r\).

Notation for (1):

  • \(\mathbf{x}[k] \in \mathbb{R}^n\): state vector; \(n\) is the state dimension (model order).

  • \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\): state matrix; its eigenvalues determine modal frequency and damping.

  • \(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C},\mathbf{D}\): input, output, and direct matrices; pulse response is \(\mathbf{h}_k = \mathbf{C} \mathbf{A}^{k-1} \mathbf{B}\).

  • \(u[k], \mathbf{y}[k]\): input and output (vector for multi-channel).

ERA vs NExT-ERA — ERA requires impulse or free-decay response (e.g. from impact tests or known input); NExT-ERA uses only response under ambient excitation, replacing the impulse response with correlation functions before running the same Hankel + SVD + realisation, so it is used for output-only operational modal analysis (e.g. bridges, buildings).

docs.title: Step 1: Data preparation and “pulse / equivalent pulse” sequence
docs.text:
ERA (with impulse or free decay):

1.1 Input: Impulse response sequence \(\mathbf{h}_0, \mathbf{h}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{h}_L\) (matrix sequence for multi-channel), or equivalent Markov parameters from free decay; sampling interval \(\Delta t\). In practice, \(L\) should cover 2–3 times the decay time of the modes of interest (e.g. for 1% damping, decay time \(\sim 1/(\zeta\omega_n)\)), so take \(L \approx \lfloor (2\sim3) \times (1/(\zeta\omega_n)) \times f_s \rfloor\).

1.2 Preprocessing: Remove DC (subtract mean per channel); optional detrend and band-pass filter (keep the band of interest); if using free decay, apply RDT or similar first for cleaner decay, then convert to Markov form.

NExT-ERA (output-only):

1.3 Input: Multi-channel response time series \(\{y_i[k]\}\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), \(k=1,\ldots,N\), sampling rate \(f_s\), \(\Delta t = 1/f_s\). Use enough samples \(N\) for stable correlation estimates (e.g. at least tens of thousands, or 2–5 minutes of data).

1.4 Estimate correlation: Choose a reference channel (e.g. \(y_{\mathrm{ref}}\), preferably high SNR and not at a node of the modes of interest). For each channel \(i\) estimate cross-correlation with reference (or auto-correlation):

\[R_{i,\mathrm{ref}}(\tau) = \frac{1}{N-\tau} \sum_{k=1}^{N-\tau} y_i[k] \, y_{\mathrm{ref}}[k+\tau], \qquad \tau = 0,1,\ldots,L. \tag{2}\]

Under white-noise excitation, \(R_{i,\mathrm{ref}}(\tau)\) is proportional to the “impulse response from reference to channel \(i\)”, so \(R_{i,\mathrm{ref}}(0), R_{i,\mathrm{ref}}(1), \ldots\) can be used as equivalent Markov parameters in the following ERA steps.

Reproducible detail (NExT-ERA): For single reference and multiple outputs, the \(k\)-th Markov block can be the column vector \(\mathbf{Y}_k = [R_{1,\mathrm{ref}}(k), \ldots, R_{n,\mathrm{ref}}(k)]^T\) (\(n\) = number of channels); for matrix form, treat \(\mathbf{Y}_k\) as an \(n\times 1\) block so each block in the Hankel is this column.

Practical notes:

  • Reference channel: choose one with good SNR and not at a node of the modes of interest; try several references and compare stabilisation diagrams.
